#3222. Which Foldable Phone Has the Best Battery Life? We Put Them to the Test

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Apple's iPhone Duo to Samsung's and Motorola's foldables, we tested how today's most popular book-style and flip phones hold up under pressure.

For years, foldable phones haven’t exactly been praised for their battery life. However, that’s starting to change.

Because of their unique design, foldables have traditionally struggled to match the battery life of conventional slab phones. Their massive displays, space-consuming hinge mechanisms and limited room for heat dissipation all present challenges. But battery technology has improved in recent years, with some of the newest foldables benefiting from higher-energy-density silicon-carbon batteries and more power-efficient processors. Even slim phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 can last all day, showing that you don’t have to sacrifice practicality for a sleek, innovative design.

Still, foldable phones remain a niche category, even with a major player like Apple entering the market with the iPhone Duo. But they offer an appealing alternative for anyone looking to break away from the sameness of more traditional slab phones. And with battery life being a key consideration when choosing a new device, it’s important to know which phone can keep up with all your scrolling, streaming and snapping without constantly reaching for a charger.

We’ve dug into CNET’s extensive smartphone lab data to find out which foldable phone in 2026 delivers the best battery life. Because book-style and flip phones differ in design and screen size, we’re separating the results to provide a more accurate comparison.

Here’s how devices from Samsung, Apple, Google and Motorola stack up.

This year, CNET has reviewed and tested five book-style foldable phones: the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Fold, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Apple iPhone Duo. These devices are phone-tablet hybrids, with designs ranging from taller, narrower builds to squatter, passport-style designs. (We didn’t include Samsung’s Galaxy Z TriFold because of its unique design.)

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo may be late to the foldable game, arriving seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold ushered in the modern era of foldable phones. Still, given Apple’s strong brand loyalty and mainstream appeal, the Duo has generated considerable buzz.

And there’s another reason Apple’s first foldable deserves attention: its battery. The iPhone Duo achieved the highest average score in CNET’s testing among book-style phones. It’s a testament to its dual-cell battery design, which is standard in foldables, and the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip powering the device.

To test a phone’s battery, CNET runs a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute endurance test that includes watching videos, scrolling through social media, playing a game and joining a video call. Both tests take place on the foldable phone’s inner screen, starting with a full charge and while connected to Wi-Fi.

The iPhone Duo had the highest remaining charge after the 45-minute endurance test, finishing with 99%. It ended the 3-hour streaming test with 84%, placing it just below the Razr Fold, Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra in that category. That average gives the Duo, which has a 4,883-mAh battery, the number-one place in our foldable battery tests.

Not far behind is the Razr Fold, Motorola’s first book-style foldable. This phone has a whopping 6,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which helped it earn one of the top spots in our battery testing.

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which is the company’s first palm-size foldable phone, just barely tops the more standard-size Z Fold 8 Ultra. Both phones are the thinnest in this ranking, which makes their results even more impressive. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when unfolded and 9.7mm when folded, and has a 4,800-mAh silicon-carbon battery. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is 4.1mm thick when open and 8.9mm when closed, and it has a 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery.

Close behind the competition is Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which has a 4,806-mAh battery. Like the other phones, including the iPhone Duo, it performed relatively better in the endurance test than in the streaming test. That suggests these devices handle shorter bursts of use well but can take a more noticeable battery hit during prolonged activities like video streaming. Even so, they should easily power through a full day of mixed use, whether you’re watching movies, scrolling through social media or taking photos.

Overall, every book-style foldable we tested demonstrated strong battery results. Beyond the numbers, our hands-on experience suggests you can get through most days without constantly worrying about your phone’s battery level. Be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth reviews for more on the everyday experience using each of these phones.

Some people may prefer the more nostalgic design of a flip phone. Motorola revived its iconic Razr brand for the smartphone era, and now has a handful of devices at varying price points to choose from. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 is another pocket-friendly choice.

These clamshell devices have less space for a battery than larger foldable and slab phones. Still, Motorola’s and Samsung’s battery specs are nothing to sniff at.

This year’s $800 Motorola Razr has a 4,800-mAh battery, the $1,100 Razr Plus has a 4,500-mAh battery and the $1,500 Razr Ultra has a 5,000-mAh battery. Meanwhile, the $1,200 Z Flip 8 has a 4,300-mAh battery. Every one of these phones uses a silicon-carbon battery to squeeze more power into a smaller design.

Impressively, the baseline Motorola Razr got the best average score in our battery testing of clamshell phones. It also had the highest result in CNET’s 3-hour streaming test among its peers and tied with the much pricier Razr Ultra in our battery endurance test. The Razr Ultra, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Razr Plus are in close succession.

Interestingly, the flip phones aren’t that far behind their book-style counterparts in our testing. One key advantage is that their smaller cover and inner displays require less power, helping them keep pace with larger foldables.

The results are also a testament to how battery technology is progressing, with the mobile industry increasingly shifting toward high-density silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack more capacity into tighter dimensions. This means that regardless of whether you choose a book-style or clamshell foldable, you can be assured that your battery won’t leave you in the lurch as you go about your day.

From the newest foldables like the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold to flip phones from Motorola and Samsung, you no longer have to sacrifice battery life for a more versatile mobile design. Today’s devices can comfortably get you through a full day of swiping, scrolling and snapping photos, even with larger screens to power.

In fact, when ranked among all the phones CNET tested this year, including non-folding options, the iPhone Duo sits among the top five performers, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max taking the top overall spot.

That’s especially important given that a major part of a foldable phone’s appeal is the ability to switch between two displays. You can quickly send a text on a smaller screen, then move to a larger one to watch a movie, for example. That versatility requires a battery capable of handling more intensive tasks like streaming and gaming, as well as extended activities like browsing and working across multiple displays.

And while the iPhone Duo and Motorola Razr topped CNET’s foldable battery tests, the other phones we evaluated weren’t far behind, highlighting just how competitive battery life has become across the leading brands. Ultimately, choosing the right foldable will come down to other factors, including camera performance, design and price.

Our testing data, combined with real-world experiences shared in our in-depth reviews, illustrates just how far foldable phones have evolved. They’re no longer just a novelty; they’ve become increasingly practical devices in their own right.

#3221. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3220. Nasdaq-100 Correction: 2 Proven Winners That Can Buck Historic Volatility

Two non-tech stocks are the perfect buys amid a 15% correction in the Nasdaq-100.

Although the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven bull market over the last four years has sent Wall Street's major stock indexes to several record highs, the last few weeks have served as a reminder that stocks can, indeed, go down. Last week, on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.74%) logged the largest single-session point decline in its storied history (1,422 points), while the Nasdaq-100 reached a nearly 15% correction in a month.

While a retracement has arguably been long overdue for high-flying tech stocks, several bargains abound within the Nasdaq-100 for patient investors. Two proven winners from outside the tech sector, Intuitive Surgical (ISRG +1.71%) and O'Reilly Automotive (ORLY -0.11%), can buck this historic volatility.

Though you can certainly find cheaper healthcare stocks, based on the price-to-earnings ratio, you'd struggle mightily to find a healthcare company with a sustained double-digit growth rate or with as large a moat as robotic-assisted surgical systems developer Intuitive Surgical.

Intuitive holds a veritable monopoly in robotic-assisted surgical systems, with more than 12,000 of its da Vinci systems installed worldwide. The relatively high cost of these systems, coupled with a lack of competition, often locks hospitals and surgical centers in as long-term customers.

What's arguably even more important than its virtual monopoly status is its revenue mix. In the early 2000s, Intuitive generated the bulk of its revenue from selling its high-priced, but mediocre-margin systems. As time has passed, higher-margin sales channels, including accessories sold with each procedure and system servicing, have grown into a majority of net sales. In short, this is a recipe for Intuitive's profits to grow even faster than its sales.

Innovation matters, too. In addition to developing new generations of the da Vinci surgical system, Intuitive debuted its minimally invasive lung biopsy system (Ion endoluminal system) in 2019. Ion procedures jumped by 31% in the latest quarter.

Intuitive Surgical stock may not be cheap, but there are several reasons it can maintain a healthy premium.

Another proven winner within the Nasdaq-100 that can buck this recent volatility is auto parts retailer O'Reilly Automotive.

Macro trends certainly favor O'Reilly. According to a May 2025 report from S&P Global Mobility (now Mobility Global (MBGL +1.12%)), the average age of vehicles in the U.S. rose to a record 12.8 years, up from an average of 11.1 years in 2012. Though newer vehicles are built to last longer, the aging of America's vehicles suggests drivers and mechanics will be relying on companies like O'Reilly Automotive to keep them in tip-top shape.

O'Reilly's success is also a function of its hub-and-spoke distribution model. The company's 32 distribution centers provide overnight access to more than 156,000 stock-keeping units (SKUs). Nearly 400 larger hub stores can also provide up to 115,000 SKUs on a same-day basis.

ORLY Shares Outstanding (Quarterly) data by YCharts.

But the one factor that's really set O'Reilly Automotive apart, at least from an investment standpoint, is its top-notch share repurchase program. Since the inception of its buyback program in January 2011, O'Reilly has spent just over $31 billion to retire 1.5 billion outstanding shares (OS). The company has reduced its OS by 62% in less than 16 years, meaningfully boosting its earnings per share in the process.

Tech-driven volatility doesn't change the investment thesis for O'Reilly Automotive one bit.

Sean Williams has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Intuitive Surgical and Mobility Global. #3219. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

#3218. Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ads will start appearing in AI Mode’s follow-up answers in the US as Google expands AI Mode ads to more countries.

Sponsored results will soon appear in responses to follow-up questions in Google’s AI Mode in the US. Google announced the change, along with plans to show ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more people, after reporting that AI Mode searches generate less revenue than traditional searches.

The company says sponsored product listings in AI Mode already get clicked about as often as organic results. For publishers, the change adds paid competition inside AI answers, which a Pew Research Center study last year found already make people less likely to click through to websites.

You’ve probably seen how this works: Type a question into Google, and an AI-generated summary often appears at the top of the page. That can mean fewer clicks on the ads below, which underpin Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

#3213. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

#3209. Sandisk Stock Has Collapsed by 65%, but It's Still Undergoing an 8-for-1 Stock Split on Nov. 19. Here's Why I'm Still Not Buying Shares Amidst This Nasdaq Market Slump.

P/E ratios can play tricks on investors when it comes to highly cyclical companies.

The Nasdaq Composite index briefly entered correction territory last week, dropping by more than 10% from its peak as the prices of artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks collapsed. Memory and storage giant Sandisk (SNDK +6.16%) has fallen 64% from its highs set only in June, after rising more than 10 times in value.

Sandisk management has scheduled a stock split to take place on Nov. 19. The flash memory maker trades at a cheap-looking price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) right now, but it just might be the most expensive stock you could buy today. Here's why I am not buying Sandisk stock despite the price dip and the upcoming stock split.

Data storage giant Western Digital bought SanDisk in 2016, but then hived it back off (with a slightly different name) in early 2025. Since then, the rapid pace of the AI infrastructure build-out has driven a massive increase in demand and a deep worldwide shortage of memory chips. Because of that, Sandisk and its peers have been able to raise their prices sharply.

Last quarter, its revenue was $11 billion, up 378% year over year, with a gross margin of 85%. Gross margin was below 30% in the same quarter a year ago. This boom has led to massive earnings growth, with $8.78 billion in earnings last quarter alone, up from barely breaking even a year prior.

That earnings inflection is why Sandisk stock was at one point up by more than 6,000% since Western Digital spun it off. Now, though, it has fallen by more than half from that peak in conjunction with the Nasdaq correction.

Many news items have accumulated since Sandisk's stock peaked in June that have caused investors to become nervous about the AI infrastructure theme.

OpenAI delayed its IPO. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave are reportedly having trouble raising funds in the debt markets. The midterm elections could have sweeping impacts on AI regulation and the pace of data center construction.

The less capital that flows into the AI companies, the less they will have to spend on memory chips from Sandisk. This narrative has taken hold of Wall Street at the moment, and it's why Sandisk stock has been falling.

When Sandisk reported its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results on Oct. 29, management guided for sequential revenue growth of around 10% in its fiscal Q2. This suggests that memory demand continues to grow, but that would be slower than fiscal Q1's 23% sequential growth. Wall Street hates slowing revenue growth.

Sandisk and its peers are all in the midst of building new facilities to manufacture more memory and grab more of the growing market. But eventually, as that additional production comes online in the quarters and years ahead, the supply of memory chips will come back in balance with demand. It may then exceed demand, creating a glut, at which point Sandisk and its cohort will run into trouble.

Sandisk's ability to implement significant price increases across its product lines over the past year and a half has led to massive earnings growth. The sharp shift in its gross margins illustrates the wild cyclicality in the memory chip market. Historically, the memory chip sector has experienced many periods of high demand and prices that were followed by equally deep declines as the supply-and-demand dynamic reversed. I don't think this time will be different.

For investors, the stock split is a meaningless event. It only increases the total number of shares outstanding, but it changes nothing about either the stock's valuation or the underlying business. Never buy shares in a company just because of a stock split.

Right now, Sandisk trades at what looks like a dirt-cheap forward price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 3.5. It is possible that Sandisk will generate the expected level of earnings that ratio is based on over the next 12 months. However, over a longer time horizon, a downturn in the memory chip market could significantly affect this earnings ratio.

If Sandisk's annualized revenues fall back to $10 billion (which is what the company was reporting less than a year ago) and its operating margin collapses from 73% to 10% as it loses its shortage-driven pricing power, its earnings will fall to $1 billion. That would give it a P/E ratio of 100 relative to the current market cap of around $100 billion. That makes Sandisk stock look wildly expensive for anyone thinking about holding it beyond the next few quarters.

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3207. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

The rollout of Uber Parking, announced on Monday, comes after the ride-hailing platform’s acquisition of SpotHero earlier this year. Now, you can reserve a parking spot from the Uber app homepage, alongside existing options to book a ride, rent a car or order a meal.

Uber says its acquisition of SpotHero is bringing more than 13,000 garages, lots and valet options across more than 400 cities onto Uber’s platform. The SpotHero brand and app won’t go away, though customers might see branding for SpotHero by Uber on garage signage, for example.

At launch, Uber Parking is available in 15 cities, including Chicago, Nashville, San Francisco, Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, Seattle and Washington, DC.

“Our mission is to help people get around, and this seemed like a very natural thing for us to solve, given how painful parking is today,” Amit Fulay, vice president of product at Uber, said in an interview. “If we can bring that ease that we have for rides into the app, it fits with helping people move. It felt like a very natural extension.”

Uber One members will get 10% back in credits on eligible completed parking reservations, which they can use on future rides and Uber Eats orders. (Uber One costs $10 per month.)

To reserve a spot with Uber Parking, open the Uber app and tap the new Parking icon on the home screen. Enter your destination, and choose a date and time. You’ll then be able to see available nearby parking options via an interactive map, which will show pricing upfront.

You can filter for options like self-parking or valet, as well as a garage or surface lot. You can also select amenities such as on-site staff or re-entry capability.

Fill out your vehicle information, including make, model and license plate number. As with booking a ride, you’ll be able to pay using a payment method in your Uber Wallet.

You’ll then be able to access your “Parking pass” in the Uber app. Depending on where you park, you’ll either scan a QR code or use license plate recognition to get in. You can extend your reservation in the app if you end up staying longer than expected.

Uber says that with most parking options, you can cancel your booking for free before the start time.

Over the coming weeks and months, Uber Parking will expand from 15 launch cities to over 400 across the US and Canada, according to the company.

Uber Parking is the latest example of how the ride-hailing company aims to be known for much more than just that. Uber now has options for everything from car and bike rentals to hotel reservations to food delivery through Uber Eats. The addition of Uber Parking gives people another reason to open the app and, importantly, give more of their dollars to Uber.

The Uber One subscription service is another way the company has worked to entice customers. It includes no delivery fee on food and grocery orders, 5% back on rides and 10% back on hotel bookings, among other perks. Uber says it has over 55 million Uber One members across 47 countries.

Uber’s new parking venture feeds into another area the company is heavily investing in: autonomous vehicles. With more than 30 AV partners, Uber says it plans to “explore leveraging parking spots as staging and waiting locations for AVs, which can reduce deadheading, congestion and vehicle wear while improving fleet efficiency.”

Fulay notes that this network can also be useful for delivery drivers working in areas where parking is difficult to find, or for those with downtime who need a convenient place to stop for a while in dense urban areas.

“Once we have this infrastructure, those are the next set of things we’ll look to explore,” Fulay said.

Ultimately, offering a service within an app consumers likely already have on their phones could make them more inclined to stick with a single company. Uber appears to be betting on just that.

#3199. Energy Transfer’s EPS Missed by 20%. Enbridge’s Profit Nearly Doubled. Here’s Why I’m Not Worried About Either Dividend Even Though Both Still Fell Short.

Energy Transfer missed estimates, and Enbridge’s profit nearly doubled, but neither headline tells you whether the dividend is safe. Here’s what the cash flow shows for each pipeline giant.

Energy Transfer's (ET +0.90%) third-quarter earnings per unit came in about 20% below analysts' expectations. A few days later, Enbridge (ENB +1.09%) reported a profit that nearly doubled from a year ago. If you judged these two pipeline giants by those headlines alone, you'd probably think one had a strong quarter, while the other did not. That would be a mistake because neither number tells you the real story, especially when it comes to the safety of their high-yielding dividends.

Here are the numbers that show why I'm not worried about these high-yielding dividend stocks.

One common mistake many investors make when analyzing pipeline stocks is putting too much emphasis on their reported earnings per share. That number isn't a true representation of the underlying earnings these companies generate. That's because pipelines and other energy infrastructure assets are capital intensive. As a result, pipeline companies often record significant depreciation charges that lower reported earnings. Additionally, gains and losses on asset sales or commodity hedges can meaningfully distort reported earnings.

A better measure of pipeline profitability is distributable cash flow (DCF). This is the cash generated by these businesses that they could distribute to investors via dividends. Here's the math for these pipeline giants

Enbridge reported GAAP earnings of 1.3 billion Canadian dollars ($920 million), or CA$0.59 per share ($0.42), in the third quarter, nearly double the year-ago period. Despite nearly doubling, Enbridge's reported earnings were still below the CA$0.97 per share ($0.69) it pays in dividends each quarter.

Enbridge's DCF, on the other hand, is more than twice the size of its reported earnings at CA$2.7 billion ($1.9 billion), a nearly 4% year-over-year increase. That puts its dividend payout ratio at 79%. It's an even more comfortable 66% based on the midpoint of the company's 2026 guidance range, well within its 60%-70% target range. That puts its nearly 6%-yielding dividend on a much firmer foundation.

That conservative payout ratio enables Enbridge to retain excess cash to reinvest in the growth of its operations. The company generates CA$5 billion to CA$6 billion ($3.6 billion to $4.3 billion) in post-dividend free cash flow each year. Enbridge can fund over CA$10 billion ($7.1 billion) in new investments each year by adding its additional balance sheet capacity while remaining within its targeted leverage ratio range. This robust investment capacity supports its expectation of growing its DCF per share by around a 5% annual rate, which should support similar dividend growth. Enbridge has increased its payout for 31 straight years (in Canadian dollars).

We see a similar story at Energy Transfer. The master limited partnership (MLP) reported GAAP earnings of $1.1 billion, or $0.33 per unit, missing the analysts' consensus estimate of $0.41 per unit by nearly 20%. Like Enbridge, Energy Transfer's reported earnings were below its current distribution level ($0.3425 per unit).

However, its DCF was much higher at $2.5 billion, a 33% increase from the prior year. That was more than double what it distributed to unit holders ($1.2 billion), putting its more than 7%-yielding payout on a much firmer foundation.

Energy Transfer's robust cash flow supports its continued expansion. The MLP plans to invest about $5.5 billion into expansion projects this year and another $7 billion in 2027. These investments should support 3% to 5% annual distribution growth. Energy Transfer has raised its payout for 20 straight quarters.

Reported earnings can make the high-yielding dividends of pipeline stocks such as Enbridge and Energy Transfer seem at risk of a reduction. However, those numbers don't show the true underlying cash-generating capabilities of these companies. When you look at their cash flows, their payouts are on much more sustainable foundations. It's why I'm not worried about either of their high-yielding dividends.

Matt DiLallo has positions in Enbridge and Energy Transfer. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Enbridge. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

#3196. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

#3194. Apple will monitor your public iCloud links now, starting with iOS 27.3

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Under Apple's new policy, the company will scan publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content - and possibly ban violators.

Be careful what you share in your iCloud. Apple announced it will start monitoring public iCloud links for harmful content — and potentially disable accounts that violate company policy.

Also: How to free up your iPhone storage almost immediately

The change comes with the impending release of Apple’s 27.3 build across its operating systems. If an iCloud user selects “Anyone with the link” when sharing something in a group chat or Discord server, it’s considered a public link; Apple is within its rights to scan for anything that violates company policy or is potentially illegal.

If you try to upload harmful content, Apple says it reserves the right to “move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” your content at any time. Furthermore, Apple outlines possible actions it may take, including:

Apple’s announcement did not explain what “harmful content” would mean in practice. While there are obvious violations like drug sales and child sex abuse material, the new policy’s vagueness is concerning.

Once an iCloud link is shared under the “Anyone with a link” designation, end-to-end encryption is removed, even if either party has enabled Advanced Data Protection, which allows Apple to view the link’s content.

If you select “People you choose,” which limits access to users who have been invited or approved, the encryption remains in place, and Apple won’t be able to see what you’re sharing.

The new policy does not lay out an appeals process if you think your account or content has been falsely flagged as harmful. However, Apple does have a web page that provides information on how to appeal for other reasons. So there is a framework in place to push back if you think you’ve been caught in the dragnet by accident.

#3193. Breakfast News: Nvidia’s Governance Moment

Here’s what worries us most about the unexpected Huang news.

When unexpected news breaks about a leader we’re invested in, we at The Motley Fool try to slow down and separate the person from the business. That’s how we’re approaching this weekend’s news from Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%).

As we know, CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. And U.S. officials have expressed concerns that she was mindfully gathering sensitive information on Nvidia’s technology and strategy for Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia’s board is now investigating. So far, the board says it has no reason to think any national security information or company secrets were compromised.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s business looks the same as it did on Friday. Many Wall Street firms have not altered their price targets, and Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co still thinks Nvidia leads China by two to three years in artificial intelligence chips.

However, we do expect substantial fallout in Washington.

Huang has spent years lobbying to sell advanced chips in China. Lawmakers from both parties now want a closer look at those sales, and the incoming Congress could move to tighten export rules again.

We’ve always viewed Nvidia’s chance for China sales as upside to our core thesis. Losing that opportunity would not alter our long-term view.

Huang has led Nvidia since 1993. Around 60 executives report to him directly. That structure leaves no obvious successor were he to step aside, even for a short leave. The board has publicly backed Huang, and we think his departure is unlikely, but shareholders will obviously want more clarity on succession now.

All told, we’re staying the course with Nvidia, a stock that our Rule Breakers team recommended at 16 cents per share in 2005 and never sold. Our Hidden Gems team bought NVDA at $5.29 in 2018 and never sold.

But the views across our teams are subject to change (not surprisingly) if the investigation shows Huang shared secrets or let Nvidia’s chips reach restricted buyers. For Fools with a position size in Nvidia greater than 15% of their net worth, we don’t see reasons to react urgently. But you might consider making some incremental sales.

Finally, if Nvidia’s board handles this well, the company should come out of it with stronger governance paired with a public succession plan. Some silver lining to a grey grey cloud.

Team Hidden Gems has a five-year price prediction of $321.42, implying an annualized return of about 12.5%.

Team Rule Breakers has a five-year price prediction of $562.47, implying an annualized return of around 26%.

CEO and co-founder Jeff Lawson did a good job steering the company through the IPO process. But the start-up mentality lost its luster. Investors started to question the

Then came Khozema Shipchandler. Though not a founder, he has held Twilio’s trifecta of top roles: CFO, then COO, and CEO since January 2024. Shares have nearly tripled since he took over.

Twilio’s investments in AI are paying off. Thanks to strong leadership and a clear vision, we think there’s still plenty of opportunity for Twilio to grow.

#3192. Bluetooth Core 7.0 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3190. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

Find out when you might be able to watch the latest entry in the 'Godzilla' movie franchise at home

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The King of the Monsters is back, and bigger than ever. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” stomped into U.S. theaters on November 6, and it's been attracting kaiju-hungry viewers ever since.

Picking up in 1949, two years after the events of the first film, the sequel continues the story of the Shikishima family in a shattered post-war Japan as they face a new threat from the towering kaiju.

The film was shot specifically for IMAX, the first Japanese production ever to do so. It’s playing in theaters right now, but how long before you can watch it from the comfort of your own couch?

Since it just hit theaters, “Godzilla Minus Zero” isn’t available on any of the best streaming services just yet. Here’s the good news, though: based on how its predecessor rolled out, we can make a solid guess about when you’ll be able to rent, buy, and stream it at home.

If you’re curious about when to start planning for a giant lizard-stomping movie night, we’ve got the answers right here. Keep reading to find out.

North American distributor GKIDS hasn’t announced a digital release date yet, but if “Godzilla Minus Zero” follows the typical pattern for a theatrical release, it should hit premium video-on-demand (PVOD) about a month after it opens, at which point you can rent or buy it on platforms like Amazon and Apple TV.

Counting forward from its November 6 release, that points to a digital debut sometime in December 2026.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Physical media is a different story. It typically follows a few weeks after the digital release. “Godzilla Minus One” got a well-regarded 4K UHD and Blu-ray release, so its sequel is likely to get the same treatment.

That means a physical release for “Godzilla Minus Zero” around January 2027 seems like a reasonable bet, though nothing has been confirmed just yet. Since it was shot for IMAX, a 4K disc will be the closest most people get to that presentation at home.

As for streaming the movie with a subscription service, our strongest clue for a release date is how the first film was handled. “Godzilla Minus One” landed on Netflix in the U.S. about six months after its theatrical release, and with Netflix having become the streaming home for that movie, its sequel seems likely to follow suit.

If it sticks to the same roughly six-month timeline, “Godzilla Minus Zero” could reach Netflix sometime around May 2027. A ways off, yes, but good things are worth waiting for.

That said, nothing about the streaming date has been officially confirmed, so the exact platform and timing could still change. For now, the only way to see Godzilla’s latest rampage is on the biggest screen you can find. And you can still enjoy the other 30+ movies in the "Godzilla" franchise while waiting.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is a direct sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” so you'll want to make sure you're caught up before watching this movie. It was set in the ashes of World War II and followed Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a former kamikaze pilot consumed by guilt after failing to act during an earlier Godzilla attack.

Back in Tokyo, he builds a family with Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and an orphaned child, only for a mutated Godzilla to rise from the sea and lay waste to the city. A group of civilian veterans ultimately got together to take the monster down and succeeded, so you'll want to watch that play out before diving into this movie.

“Minus Zero” picks the story back up in 1949, two years after those events. The Shikishima family has started to rebuild amid a Japan still struggling to recover, but the peace doesn’t last, and Godzilla returns to threaten the country once again.

With the memory of the last devastation still fresh, a disaster-response team scrambles to prepare for the renewed menace, and the Shikishimas are pulled right back into the fight for survival. And yes, it's just as epic in scale as the last movie, so you'll want to catch this one whether you see it at home or on the big screen.

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.
