#3187. How to Use AI Tools Like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to Prep for a Job Interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

AI makes it easy to rehearse a job interview as many times as you need, with feedback after every answer.

ChatGPT’s voice mode lets you run a spoken mock interview and hear follow-up questions in real time.

For job seekers, the job interview can feel like an endurance test of their skills and personality.

It’s enough to make a person yearn for the simpler days of newspaper ads and in-person handshakes. But alas, we find ourselves immersed in the era of smart homes and Bluetooth-enabled blueberry mint vapes. But AI offers one practical advantage: a way to rehearse before the real thing.

A chatbot can play the role of a hiring manager, ask questions likely to come up for a specific job and tell you — bluntly, if you want — where your answers fall flat. That makes AI chatbots some of the more practical interview prep tools available, especially since you can rehearse as many times as you need without leaning on a friend’s patience. These chatbots can also help you research the company, prepare stories that answer common behavioral questions and get a rough sense of what the role should pay.

Here are a couple of ways you can leverage AI tools to ace your next job interview.

Read more: The New Age of Hiring: AI Is Changing the Game for Job Seekers

How you look in a job interview matters. Even if you’re sitting at home pantsless and just woke up from a nap, you gotta look the part on Zoom.

You can ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to generate Zoom backgrounds that showcase your understanding of and affinity for the company culture.

Gemini created these backgrounds for my theoretical job interviews with Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Netflix and more.

Some of them turned out a little better than others, but you get the idea.

Some states, like California, have made it all but mandatory for employers to post the salary range for jobs they post as vacant. Even if you might know the salary range of the job going into the interview, the topic of compensation is always best approached with as much information as possible.

I asked Google’s Gemini AI to reference Glassdoor listings, public earnings, expenditure announcements, shareholder communications, and online media results for the salary ranges of the CEOs at Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Netflix, and Alphabet and to provide me with salary ranges for mid-level marketing professionals at those companies.

Gemini then gave me a five-year growth schedule, where it laid out how I could begin to make more money by leveraging my sign-on bonus in the first year, my vesting stock in the second, a raise in the third, a title change in the fourth and a big promotion in the fifth (very idealistic, but it could happen).

Gemini also provided more information on how each of those companies typically structures your compensation — whether it’s an all-cash salary, one with built-in bonuses, or employee stock options. It’s important to have this information when you’re asked about the salary you expect.

Most guides on how to land a gig suggest that job seekers research the company, its culture and what the role entails. But honestly, job seekers are already investing a tremendous amount of time applying to open positions and going through multiple rounds of interviews.

What’s more important is your ability to effectively explain why you’re perfect for the job.

For my hypothetical marketing role, I used Claude to research the CMOs at those companies, including their social posts and their teams’ major priorities. I asked the AI tool to give me some one-word anchors for interview talking points, cross-referenced to elements of my resume that would be directly applicable.

It gave me some keywords to bring up, and how to relate them back to my own resume, listed out CEOs’ vision and products, told me which company could be my biggest opportunity and best fit and why — and how to express that in an interview:

Nerves are normal in a high-stakes communication like a job interview. You’re trying to appear interested but not desperate, competent but not cocky, and decide on a salary requirement you won’t live to regret.

One way to get your mind right for the job interview and take the edge off could be using an AI tool to run through some sample interview questions with you.

Several online platforms offer features that let you run a trial before your interview, including Final Round AI, which offers real-time interview transcription and support, mock interviews and resume building. Another platform, Yoodli, focuses on AI-powered communication coaching to improve both verbal and nonverbal delivery and offers AI roleplays. You can also talk with Gemini Live and get real-time responses.

In my case, I asked ChatGPT via the voice chat feature to pretend it was the hiring manager for a job at a fictitious company that sells subscription dog-sitting services, and to act as if it was unimpressed by my resume to give me a challenge and desensitize me to the worst-case scenario.

While the text chat was more of a critique of my resume, bless its sweet little machine algorithm, ChatGPT in voice chat was way too nice to even get into character for this challenge, no matter how I prompted it.

AI tools can be effective options for job seekers who don’t feel comfortable reaching out to someone in their network to help them prepare. Always keep in mind, however, that AI tools come with pitfalls, including issues related to data collection, bias and inconsistent messaging.

Use AI to prepare, but don’t let it fake your performance. AI doesn’t replace genuine networking, and the guiding principle should be to stay authentic.

#3186. Prediction: Here's How Much SpaceX Will Be Worth by the End of 2027

It's been a wild ride for the stock since its historic blockbuster IPO earlier this year.

Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +5.81%), or SpaceX for short, pulled off a historic $1.77 trillion initial public offering just months ago. There have been some ups and downs early on, but today shares trade at $134, almost a bullseye on its $135 IPO price.

The company recently posted impressive growth with its Q3 2026 earnings. As a result, I predict that SpaceX stock could run 65% from here, closing 2027 at around $250 per share.

A word of caution: the artificial intelligence landscape is changing quickly, and some storm clouds could be on the horizon.

For all the attention SpaceX receives for launching rockets into space, the company operates three distinct business segments. Beyond the Space segment, investors will also find the Connectivity business, which holds Starlink, as well as the Super Intelligence (AI) segment, which houses xAI and Cursor.

SpaceX is selling compute to other AI hyperscalers, and business is booming. Management guided for Q1 2027 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion, implying the size of the business as a whole could more than double over the next six months.

SpaceX's fundamentals are changing quickly, making it that much more challenging for investors to gauge how attractive the stock is today. Suppose SpaceX hits the high end of its Q1 2027 guidance. Annualize that, and you get to roughly $150 billion in 2027 revenue.

At 20 times this hypothetical 2027 revenue, shares would trade at that $250 target. SpaceX's market cap would come in around $3.4 trillion. In other words, it would be one of the world's most valuable companies. It's worth noting that no other company, save Nvidia, is growing so quickly at such a large size.

There's also suddenly some political risk here, too. CEO Elon Musk has been a close ally of President Donald Trump for most of the past few years. Naturally, Musk has a target on his back as the world's wealthiest individual. Democrats reclaimed control of the U.S. House and Senate following the recent midterm elections.

Voters came out in force against various data center proposals, and some politicians have already made it clear they intend to scrutinize AI companies more closely. This could become a big challenge for SpaceX, which is now counting on its AI computing business to achieve the blistering growth it's guiding for.

Despite all this, Wall Street analysts remain bullish on SpaceX. There are 47 analyst ratings on CNN Business, with a median 12-month price target of $245 -- right around my prediction. But don't forget that things can change quickly.

Owning SpaceX is essentially a vote of confidence in Musk's ability to lead the company through this increasingly complex AI revolution while simultaneously delivering on lofty growth goals. There might not be a riskier stock at its market cap, but the upside is there if SpaceX delivers.

#3184. Adobe unveils new AI tools for Photoshop, Premiere, and more, with MCP support coming in 2027

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving users more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the company unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets users** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two new AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” says the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a new color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”

Another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe announced that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps users find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more quickly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

As for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more quickly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add new files to a Google Drive folder, update the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

The company notes that MCP integrations will enter private beta in early 2027, and users can sign up here to learn more.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping users organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Plan Mode, which lets users review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when users step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

These assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the company’s blog.

This flying home security camera has been in the works for a while

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After years in the works, Ring's flying home security camera drone is finally taking flight. The Ring Drone Cam, as it's called, has gone through several iterations since the company first introduced it as the Ring Always Home cam three years ago.

Now that Ring is ready to ship the device, it gave us a sneak preview in advance. Here's my initial impressions of the Ring Drone Cam, as well as how much it'll cost, and when you can get one for your home.

Unlike the Always Home Cam, which had a large protuberance on its underside, the Ring Drone Cam looks somewhat like the DJI Neo; it has a small rectangular body with four encaged rotors. Weighing 265 grams (5.8 ounces), it's lighter than most phones. While the demo unit I saw was white, the actual product will be a light gray. The Drone Cam docks and recharges in a square base station.

The drone has a 2K camera with two LEDs on either side, which it uses to light up your home as it's patrolling at night.

When activated, the Drone Cam lifts up out of its base, rises to about 4-5 feet in the air, and then proceeds at a stately pace as it moves throughout your home. Even though it's small, you'll definitely notice its presence, as its rotors make a very loud, high-pitched whine.

Knowing how my dog reacts to a vacuum cleaner, I can only imagine his response to this thing flying around the house. Don't even ask what my cats might think.

The Drone Cam navigates your home using a combination of an Alexa Home map (similar to what you'll see on one of Amazon's smart displays) and the setup process, whereby you hold the drone and carry it through your house, taking it on a trip of where you'd like to go. Ring says the Drone Cam can cover multiple stories of your home.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Unlike previous, unreleased versions, the Drone Cam relies on the cloud for navigation, using Amazon's AI Pilot to get around and interpret what the drone is seeing. If the drone loses its connection, it's designed to immediately land — which is why it's important that you make sure its flight path doesn't go over any delicate objects.

The Ring Drone Cam can be programmed to make regular patrols of your house, or to respond to a particular event — such as a window or a door sensor tripping, or a water leak detector going off. Using the Amazon Alexa Home map, it can fly to the location of the event, and give you a live view of what's happening.

Remember the Amazon Astro? Ring took its parent company's home robot and redesigned the internals to make it a security robot for small businesses and enterprise customers.

Now called the Ring Rover Cam, it's meant to patrol warehouses and stores, and alert you if it detects an intruder. Like the Astro, it has a telescoping camera, but Ring also added a light on the back, which lets you see where the robot is at a glance, and flashes red and screams out a siren when there's an unwanted guest.

The Ring Rover Cam will cost $999, and will ship on December 16.

I am more than a bit skeptical about having a camera drone flying through my house. For starters, my pets get nervous enough around vacuum cleaners; I can only imagine how they'd react to a high-pitched drone flying about. And, the idea of a drone autonomously roaming around, potentially recording everything, feels a bit dystopian.

And, if you want the Ring Drone Camera to be able to access every corner of your house, you'll also have to make sure you leave every door wide open before you leave. And, the drone moves so slowly that if it's set up on one side of your house, by the time it responds to, say, a window breaking on the other side, the potential intruder could be long gone.

I can see some utility in it — I don't have, nor do I want, security cameras in every corner of my house, so I can see it being handy if a sensor is tripped in my basement. But, I'm still not sold on the concept; maybe trying it out will change my mind.

What do you think? Would you want a drone security camera for the inside of your house? Take our poll, and let me know in the comments.

#3182. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3181. NASA’s Voyager 1 to Cross Historic One Light-Day Milestone on Nov. 18

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Traveling one light-day took the space probe 49 years. it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is on track to set another historic record as its mission approaches the half-century mark. On Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. ET, the probe will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, a journey of nearly five decades that places it farther from our planet than any human-made object in history.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster than that. It currently zips along the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after its previous one, when Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after passing Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the life of Voyager 1. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s life-span.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called The Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for any signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three remaining instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two instruments still in operation.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, the RTGs now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Thanks to the vastness of space, Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3178. Aura Ink 10 review: A digital photo frame that looks (almost) like a real picture

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

The Aura Ink 10 is a second-generation ePaper photo frame that’s smaller and less expensive than the original, and can display a few more colors. If you’re looking for a digital photo frame you can hang on your wall without any wires showing, this is the one to get, though it is more expensive than most other frames, and overall it's less vibrant than a traditional digital photo frame.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

A year ago, Aura introduced the Aura Ink, the first ePaper photo frame; this device, while not as vibrant as a traditional digital photo frame, had the advantage of letting you hang it on a wall — no power cord required — for up to three months at a time without needing to be recharged.

The company is back with the Aura Ink 10, the first in the second generation of ePaper style photo frames. This frame can show more colors, and at $349, is also less expensive, albeit still well above some of the best digital photo frames. So, is the premium worth it?

The Aura Ink 10 went on sale on November 10, 2026, for $349 at Aura's website. It’s offered in just one size, and with just one matte color (black). The original only came with a white matte; I wish the company offered both options.

The frame itself is very thin, at a little less than an inch, and comes with both a stand for placing it on a table, as well as pins so you can mount it on a wall. Three buttons sit inconspicuously on the back edge of the frame, and let you switch photos and get the frame ready to go. Overall, it’s a very subtle design, and it’s unlikely that anyone would recognize it as a digital frame at a glance.

The Aura Ink 10 uses an E Ink Spectra 6 display, which can produce nine colors (black, white, red, yellow, blue, green, off-white, mustard yellow and orange), up from six on the original Aura Ink. That means it can show more nuances in pictures, though don’t expect true-to-life fidelity that you would get from a traditional LCD picture frame. The 10-inch frame also has the same resolution as the 13-inch model, which means greater pixel density.

To see the difference in Aura Ink generations, I placed the 10-inch Ink next to the 13-inch Ink, and then displayed the same photos on each.

The 10 inch model tended to show photos a little darker, but with better transitions between light and dark areas. For example, in an image of a girl jumping off a sand dune, there was less obvious pixelation from the sun-drenched stretches of the beach to shaded areas.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In another photo of a girl in front of a blue and white wall, the blues of the wall were a bit deeper, but shadows were more pronounced, making it more difficult to make out features in her face and neck area.

The Aura Ink 10 has very gentle lighting that only turns on if it senses someone in front of the frame. Again, it’s not something you’d notice unless you see it turn on, but it helps bring a little more vibrancy to the photo.

Aura says the Ink 10 will last up to three months on a charge, assuming it changes photos just once per day. Once it runs low, you simply have to plug it into a USB-C for a little bit.

Aura also updated the manner in which the frame refreshes; on the original model, the screen kind of flashes randomly as the photo changes. On the Ink 10, there’s a wave-like pattern that starts in one corner, and ripples across the screen. It’s more intentional, and doesn’t make it look like the frame is shorting out.

One thing that Aura does well is make it easy to add photos to its devices. For starters, you can sync your iCloud or Google Photos albums in the Aura app. And, to help narrow things down, the Aura app can filter photos by person, so that you can more easily find photos of particular individuals; unfortunately, there’s no pet filter. If you want to skip the app entirely, you can also either email or text photos to the display. Handy!

As someone who tests smart home devices for a living, I suspect my house, which has smart displays everywhere, is a bit different than most. So while I appreciate traditional digital photo frames — the Alexa Photo Frame is one of my favorites, for its innovative use of AI — it’s nice to have some tech that doesn’t look like tech.

Yes, there are some tradeoffs to an ePaper photo display like the Aura Ink 10. You’re not going to get colors that really fly off the screen, and you’re going to pay a premium over other photo frames. But, in a digital-everything world, I appreciate its subtleness.

#3174. CME vs. S&P Global: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Two financial giants, one a derivatives powerhouse and the other a ratings and data leader, with very different risk profiles for 2027.

Choosing between CME Group (CME -0.45%) and S&P Global (SPGI +0.70%) involves weighing the world's leading derivatives marketplace against the preeminent provider of credit ratings and financial data. Which is the better buy today?

Both companies are infrastructure giants in the financial world. CME processes trillions in trades, while S&P Global provides the ratings and analytics that keep capital flowing. Investors often look to these financial stocks for stability, but their business models offer different exposures to market volatility and economic growth.

CME Group operates the world's leading derivatives marketplace, enabling clients to trade futures and options across asset classes like energy and agriculture. The company serves various participants among financial stocks, including central banks. It maintains a technology partnership with Google Cloud and a joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT +0.35%). In 2025, one company accounted for 12% of CME's clearing and transaction fee revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, representing growth of roughly 6.4% over the previous year. Net income was close to $4 billion. The net margin was approximately 62%, which shows the percentage of revenue remaining after all operating and non-operating costs are paid.

As of CME's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.1. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, indicating a very low reliance on borrowed funds. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is approximately 1. Free cash flow reached nearly $4.2 billion, representing the cash remaining after the company pays for its capital expenditures.

S&P Global provides essential credit ratings, benchmarks, and analytics that facilitate global capital and commodity markets. Its business is highly diversified, with segments ranging from market intelligence to mobility and energy data. The company serves a global customer base including asset managers and automotive manufacturers through both third-party and proprietary distribution channels. This broad reach ensures its ratings and indexes remain standard tools for investors worldwide.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $15.3 billion, representing growth of close to 7.9% over the prior year. Net income was approximately $4.5 billion. The net margin was roughly 29.2%, indicating that the company retains nearly $0.30 of profit for every dollar of revenue generated.

On S&P Global's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.5. The current ratio is roughly 0.8. Free cash flow for the period was close to $5.5 billion.

CME Group faces risks from global economic and political conditions that can significantly impact trading volumes. The company is subject to intense competition from other exchanges, over-the-counter markets, and digital asset platforms. Regulatory and compliance risks are also high, including potential new transaction taxes and oversight of prediction market activities. Operational risks include heavy reliance on third-party providers such as Google Cloud and the potential failure of clearing firms.

S&P Global faces significant cybersecurity and technology risks as a central provider of market data. The business is sensitive to interest rate fluctuations and market volatility, which can reduce the volume of new debt issuance. Competitive risks come from both traditional and non-traditional data providers, while regulatory oversight of credit rating agencies remains intense. It also faces operational risks from its reliance on third-party infrastructure providers such as Amazon (AMZN +2.94%) and the complexity of its planned segment separations.

CME Group has a lower forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, while S&P Global maintains a lower P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

CME Group's revenue growth is pretty uninspiring, but S&P Global's isn't significantly higher. Furthermore, CME pays a higher-yielding dividend. But I think the most attractive thing about the derivatives specialist is its net margin. CME's 62% net margin is basically twice what S&P Global reported in fiscal 2025.

Past performance is no indication of future results, of course. But CME Group stock has trailed S&P Global by more than 100 percentage points over the past 10 years. Indeed, CME hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500.

An impressive net margin and a modest dividend are nice, but ultimately I want a stock that will increase in value. (Pretty core investing concept!) If CME Group hasn't beaten the market over the past decade, why should I have any expectation that trend will reverse itself now? S&P Global gets my vote here.

#3172. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3171. Bill Ackman and Warren Buffett Both Have the Same Warning About the Stock Market

The billionaire investors both see the stock market behaving more like a casino of late.

Some of the smartest, most experienced investors in the world are concerned about the markets right now. While the S&P 500 (^GSPC +2.35%) has continued to do well this year, rising by 10% and hitting new records along the way, it hasn't been an entirely smooth ride. Plus, with stock valuations remaining elevated, there's the risk that there may still be a large pullback looming.

Bill Ackman and Warren Buffett are among the most well-known and successful investors in the world, and both are seeing cause for concern in the stock market. They've also issued similar warnings about the market this year, suggesting there's too much risk-taking and gambling going on.

In a recent interview with CNBC, Ackman pointed to the nonsensical prices that many stocks trade at, stating that, "stocks trade at prices that make no sense to me" and that "we're back to the casino-type markets when there was 95% leverage."

This sounds remarkably similar to the warning Buffett issued months earlier about the difficulties in finding stocks to buy given their egregious valuations. "It's tough to find values when everybody is preferring gambling." Buffett, the former Berkshire Hathaway CEO, has in recent years mentioned the inability to find good deals in the markets and not seeing a whole lot to buy. Now, with the S&P 500 on track to deliver a 10% gain or better for the fourth consecutive year, it may be more difficult than ever to do that.

Many stocks have been soaring to incredibly high valuations even though they don't appear to be justified given their underlying financials. Space Exploration Technologies Corp with its roughly $2 trillion market cap, stands out as an obvious example, as does Palantir Technologies, which trades at more than 100 times its earnings.

Buying these types of stocks at mammoth premiums opens investors up to the risk of corrections later on. It's important for investors to be prudent and disciplined when investing in stocks to ensure they aren't just chasing hot trends that may end up fizzling out later on.

For long-term investors, the safest move may be to simply track the S&P 500 through index funds these days. Ackman and Buffett's warnings, however, shouldn't be ignored, as there are definitely reasons for investors to exercise caution these days.

#3170. iOS 27.3 Could Bring More Audio Intelligence and the Redesigned Health App Soon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The Health app overhaul and new Apple Intelligence features lead the latest public beta.

Apple launched the first public beta of iOS 27.3 on Monday, about two months after the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iOS 27. The headliner here is the return of the new Health app: After briefly testing the redesigned Health app in an early iOS 27.2 beta, Apple has put the app back in the recent beta cycle.

Apple historically releases an iOS update in December, so I expect iOS 27.3 to land on iPhones later this year.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.3, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short, so it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, there could be more features to land on your iPhone when Apple releases 27.3.

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the first iOS 27.3 beta.

The redesigned Health app returns in the iOS 27.3 beta after Apple tested the feature in the iOS 27.2 beta process. Developers and beta testers can explore the refreshed app and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

Apple wrote online that we can expect the redesigned Health app to land on devices later this year.

If developers and beta testers have an Apple Watch that is running the watchOS 27.3 beta as well as an iPhone running the iOS 27.3 beta, those folks can test out Apple’s Live Rewind and Siri Recap in Audio Intelligence.

Live Rewind allows you to pull up a text transcript of a conversation in the past 15 seconds on your Apple Watch, and Siri Recap can automatically give you a summary of meetings, conversations and other events. Live Rewind snippets are replaced by new audio and then deleted, and Siri Recaps delete themselves after seven days if you don’t manually delete them sooner. However, you can also save both of these in the Siri app and export them to the Notes or Journal apps on your iPhone.

While both Live Rewind and Siri Recap are automatically deleted over time, I’m uncomfortable with the ability to save snippets or recaps, which raises concerns about people recording my conversations without my knowledge. Even if Audio Intelligence just summarizes what I said, I still find both features creepy.

And while I recognize the utility for certain groups of people, I also think it’s better to just, y’know… talk to someone instead of asking your watch what they just said.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets and weights in order to help you meet your goals. And if you’re unfamiliar with an exercise, you can also watch video tutorials to see how to perform that exercise.

Siri AI gets a huge update in the iOS 27.3 beta. The feature can now do more actions in supported apps, like Apple Music and Messages. For example, if you go into Apple Music, you can ask Siri to create a playlist for you, and in Messages, you can ask Siri to schedule, edit or unsend messages. If you open an app and ask Siri what it can do in the app, the digital assistant should give you some examples of its capabilities.

The beta also brings Siri AI to traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish and Norwegian.

StandBy mode also gets an upgrade in the iOS 27.3 beta. In the beta, you can add full weather and calendar slides to the mode and choose from more colors.

Apple introduced StandBy mode alongside iOS 17, and it was one of my favorite iPhone features. I’m happy Apple is finally showing it some love and adding more features and capabilities so it feels more like a home or desk hub.

If you’re a fan of dark mode, the iOS 27.3 beta has a treat for you. The beta gives you a new setting in Safari called Adaptive Dark Mode. When enabled, it forces dark mode onto webpages in Safari that may not have a dark mode option otherwise.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps.3. Tap Safari.4. Tap Adaptive Dark Mode.5. Tap On.

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the first beta of iOS 27.3. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.3 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices before the end of the year.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2, why you may have missed iOS 27.1 and our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

#3168. Coca-Cola's Dividend Has Grown 64 Years in a Row. I'd Buy It in November and Never Sell.

The same formula for success has worked for more than six decades, and it should continue to do so.

If you want to know why so many investors, including the great Warren Buffett, love Coca-Cola (KO +0.38%) stock, look no further than the company's impressive dividend history. The global beverage giant has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years.

A streak that long doesn't happen by accident. Coca-Cola has battled through mistakes, recessions, up-and-down markets, and even a global pandemic over the past six decades.

That's ultimately why Coca-Cola is precisely the type of stock an investor can buy in November and hold indefinitely without losing a wink of sleep at night.

Coca-Cola's empire stretches well beyond its namesake soda, including 32 brands with at least $1 billion in annual sales. It sells 2.2 billion servings of its products each day across more than 200 countries.

All those microtransactions add up to a size and scale that other companies struggle to compete with. It has an unmatched distribution network, putting Coca-Cola products on the best shelves at countless stores, in venues, and in vending machines.

The company has various paths to the steady growth it seems to produce year in and year out, decade after decade.

Coca-Cola has responded well to changing consumer preferences over the years, leaning into zero-sugar brands to appease health-conscious consumers. It launches new flavors and acquires up-and-coming brands to expand its portfolio. Of course, it can simply raise prices directly or through creative packaging and serving sizes.

And don't forget that population growth means more potential customers. Add it all up, and Coca-Cola doesn't have down years because it's a highly diversified business with a laundry list of ways to make more money, and it wields one of the world's most recognizable and beloved brand names.

Coca-Cola's revenue grew by 7% in Q3 2026, including global volume growth of 5%. Management now anticipates the company will grow comparable earnings by 11% in 2026 and generate over $13 billion in free cash flow. That puts the dividend at about 70% of guided 2026 cash flow, leaving a solid cushion and room for growth.

Analysts estimate that Coca-Cola will grow its earnings by an average of 7%-8% over the next three to five years. It's almost boring, but that's what this stock does. It delivers steady growth each year, with very little risk of catastrophe.

Perhaps the best news yet is that Coca-Cola still has plenty of room to continue expanding in a vast and fragmented global market. Management estimates that Coca-Cola still only holds a 14% share in developed markets and 6% in emerging markets.

It's generally a bad idea to buy and forget any stock, but Coca-Cola is arguably an exception. That's because the stock does its best work over the course of years, even decades. To maximize your return on Coca-Cola stock, you'll want to reinvest its famous dividend.

Reinvesting dividends means immediately pumping that dividend back into the stock for more shares that, you guessed it, also pay dividends. It adds an entire new compounding effect that makes a tremendous difference over time.

When you start measuring in decades, reinvesting the dividend can literally multiply your total returns. There's no reason to believe this formula can't still work, making Coca-Cola a no-brainer for any buy-and-hold dividend investor.

#3167. AI-Driven Tech Layoffs Could Trigger a 1.6 Million Job Recession

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With more than 200,000 job cuts in the tech industry in 2026, the bigger question is if layoffs will spread to retail and finance.

When Meta began laying off 8,000 people in May, it felt like an omen. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, had seen several high-profile failures, from the death of the metaverse to its multibillion-dollar court setbacks. The Magnificent Seven — the tech giants that drive US stock market gains — seemed to hit a plateau over the last year, as more investors expressed concern about a potential AI bubble.

A wave of recent tech layoffs and buyouts reveals a growing volatility in the tech industry, as major companies restructure to cut costs and redirect spending toward AI. In just the last few weeks, Google extended its voluntary buyout program to select employees in five countries, and the graphic design platform Canva reduced its staff by 22%, laying off or relocating 1,271 employees.

Companies that have laid off or offered buyouts to 1,000 or more employees this year include Microsoft (60,000), Oracle (21,000), Amazon (17,000 in addition to 14,000 in 2025), Uber (3,300) and Netflix (1,000). According to the TrueUp tech layoffs tracker, layoffs are accelerating faster than last year, with over 200,000 workers reduced so far in 2026. The cuts aren’t limited to struggling companies, but are affecting profitable organizations with strong revenues.

The dominant factor behind layoffs has been AI. Companies have spent billions of dollars on the technology, plus a terrifying $3.2 trillion (with a “T”) that, Goldman Sachs says, doesn’t show up on balance sheets. With current returns failing to justify the massive scale of capital expenditure, companies are slashing labor costs and relying on AI to offset the resulting productivity losses.

While the US isn’t officially in a recession (yet), there are growing fears that mass layoffs could spread to other sectors, such as retailers and financial companies, creating a large wave of workforce reductions in the country. Analysts warn that if job losses extend beyond the tech industry, it could result in another 1.6 million people being laid off, bringing the formal unemployment rate closer to recession-level.

With several economic pressures at play — inflation, higher interest rates and rising energy and computing costs — buyouts and layoffs allow company executives to reduce operating expenses while investing heavily in AI infrastructure, automation and specialized technical talent. That hasn’t worked out in all cases. A handful of companies, including Salesforce and Ford, ended up rehiring or hiring new people after AI-driven layoffs.

Even companies currently reducing their workforce, such as Canva, appear to be offering friendly terms, potentially to avoid burning bridges. As part of its severance package, Canva gave outgoing employees $10,000 grants, MacBooks, six months of salary and a year of healthcare. For many workers without a union contract, that will be the best-case scenario if the economy goes south.

Canva’s terms for departing employees are both exceedingly generous and a window into modern tech:* Six months salary* A year healthcare* A year of LinkedIn premium* A $10k grant to start a business* Keep your MacBook https://t.co/Hqdegdb8Ek pic.twitter.com/pKuj8lJDvB

Job instability, stagnant wages and rising prices have been the norm for several years, arguably since the last major US recession in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. Given that recessions historically occur about every six years (regardless of which party is in the White House), a larger downturn could be on the horizon, especially if an AI market correction triggers further stock declines and widespread layoffs. If high-cost data centers lose clients and major IPOs falter, enterprises will likely slash spending and jobs as the promise of AI-driven efficiency fades.

So far, layoffs don’t appear to be spreading to other industries, and overall job cuts are the lowest since 2022. But the job market has become increasingly precarious, especially for younger workers, according to Lisa Countryman-Quiroz, CEO of JVS Bay Area, a workforce nonprofit.

For example, entry-level hires are down by a third in the most AI-exposed occupations since 2021, which could affect sectors like retail and finance —typical entry-level gateways for many young people. Household wages aren’t keeping up with expenses, and many job seekers have found themselves unemployed for more than six months. “While we may or may not see broadening layoffs, I’m concerned about the erosion of stable career pathways,” Countryman-Quiroz said. The one bright spot seems to be in healthcare, with 42,000 jobs added last month.

The 2026 midterm elections could also indirectly affect tech layoffs, mainly due to changes in the political and regulatory environment around AI and data centers. In the lead-up to the midterms, the backlash against data centers and tech billionaires became a pressing issue for candidates. Campaigns around data center moratoriums helped some Democratic candidates, including Gina Hinojosa, the surprise gubernatorial winner in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has his home and business headquarters.

Pausing new data center construction will be a shot in the arm for communities protesting the drain of AI infrastructure on local resources. But any slowdown in the buildout could also reduce demand for construction, chip suppliers or technical roles tied to AI expansion.

The midterm elections also affected financial markets, with technology and AI-linked stocks falling as investors worried that Democrats might impose new guardrails on AI. A weaker market can often make companies more cautious about hiring, capital spending and staffing, which could exacerbate cost-cutting pressures and lead to more layoffs and buyouts.

Countryman-Quiroz suggested that Congress could address AI’s disruption by investing in more job training, especially in growing areas like healthcare. “Current federal funding is only sufficient to train about 200,000 workers per year, a fraction of what’s needed,” she said. “Workforce development has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, so there is an opportunity for both parties to work together on solutions.”

#3166. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

#3165. CME vs. PayPal: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Two exchange-style rivals -- one a derivatives powerhouse with a 62% net margin, the other a payments giant trading at a far lower multiple -- and a tougher choice than it looks.

While digital payments reshape retail, global financial markets rely on stable exchanges. Deciding between CME Group (CME -0.45%) and PayPal (PYPL +1.37%) requires weighing high-margin stability against massive scale and a value-oriented valuation.

CME Group operates major derivatives marketplaces, benefiting from volatility in interest rates and commodities. PayPal remains a leader in digital wallets and branded checkout services. We're comparing these two companies because they represent different corners of the financial world, offering distinct risk-reward profiles for investors looking toward 2027.

CME Group operates the leading marketplace for derivatives, which are financial contracts that derive value from underlying assets. As a prominent player among financial stocks, it serves professional traders and global institutions across asset classes like interest rates, energy, and metals. The company relies on a member-based model in which exchange members drive 85% of derivatives volume, and it maintains a strategic partnership with S&P Global (SPGI +0.70%) for index-based products. In addition to traditional assets, the company offers products like Bitcoin (BTC -1.16%) futures and prediction markets through a venture with FanDuel, a subsidiary of Flutter Entertainment (FLUT +0.35%).

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 6.4% compared to the prior year. The company generated net income of roughly $4 billion. This resulted in a strong net margin of about 62%. Customer concentration is a factor to watch, as one clearing firm accounts for nearly 12% of CME's clearing and transaction fee revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, was approximately 0.1. The current ratio, which gauges the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was about 1. During fiscal 2025, the business generated free cash flow of nearly $4.2 billion. Free cash flow is the cash a company generates after accounting for the money needed to maintain or expand its asset base.

PayPal operates a massive two-sided network with nearly 439 million active accounts across approximately 200 markets. The company provides a wide range of services, including Venmo for person-to-person transfers and buy now, pay later solutions for shoppers. It generates revenue by providing payment processing and fraud prevention tools to millions of merchants globally. By maintaining a lead in branded checkout, the company remains a central figure in the global digital economy.

In fiscal 2025, PayPal reported revenue of nearly $33.2 billion, an increase of approximately 4.3% from the previous year. The company achieved net income of close to $5.2 billion. These results produced a net margin of roughly 15.8%. While revenue growth has slowed compared to earlier years, PayPal continues to generate significant profits from its vast transaction volume.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was approximately 1.3. The debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.5. PayPal generated free cash flow of close to $5.6 billion during fiscal 2025. This strong cash generation provides the company with flexibility to reinvest or return value to shareholders.

CME Group is subject to risks from global market and geopolitical volatility, which can negatively impact trading volumes and revenue. The company also faces intense competition from traditional exchanges like Cboe Global Markets (CBOE -0.14%) and Deutsche Börse (DBOEF +0.60%). Furthermore, the business carries heavy regulatory burdens and operational dependency on third-party data centers, where any disruption could lead to financial loss.

PayPal operates in the highly competitive global payments industry, facing pressure from larger tech-enabled players and nimble start-ups. The company must manage significant cybersecurity risks, including potential data breaches and system outages that could harm its reputation. Additionally, PayPal faces material legal exposure from ongoing securities fraud class action litigation and evolving global regulatory scrutiny regarding consumer protection and digital assets.

PayPal appears significantly more attractive on a valuation basis, as it trades at a much lower multiple of both sales and future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The P/S ratio measures a company's market value against its sales over the past 12 months. The forward P/E ratio compares the stock price to future earnings estimates for the next year.

PayPal's valuation is clearly lower than CME Group's; investors evidently don't see the former growing much from here. While I don't think historical stock performance necessarily dictates future performance, PayPal's returns over the past 10 years don't compare favorably with CME Group's:

Over the past decade, CME Group has outperformed PayPal by more than 140 percentage points. In fact, PayPal's returns barely outpaced inflation during that period. The payments titan has been a pretty disappointing investment.

However, that chart also reveals something unflattering about both companies' share performance: Neither PayPal nor CME Group managed to keep pace with the S&P 500 over that time frame.

That said, this article is about comparing two financial stocks, not two stocks and an index. Between PayPal and CME Group, I think the derivatives specialist looks like the more attractive investment. CME Group has slightly stronger revenue growth and a significantly higher net margin, and that's why it's getting my vote today.

#3164. Ford Just Proved Its EV Battery Health Barely Degrades After 5 Years

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

2021 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs have kept most of their battery and range after thousands of miles on the road.

Real-world battery life for phones, laptops and other electronic devices can diminish over years of use, but does the same happen to electric cars after thousands of miles and hundreds of recharges? According to data published by Ford this week: Yes, but not as badly as you might fear.

The automaker published a report analyzing the battery state of health of more than 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs sold to customers across the US and Canada during the initial 2021 model year. After more than five years on the road — and an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven — the fleet averaged 92% battery health.

I call that impressive, but not totally surprising. That battery durability data is largely in line with what I’ve seen reported across the industry by other automakers and independent analysts.

One of the biggest concerns of early EV adopters a decade ago (also shared by fence-sitters today) is long-term reliability. The battery is by far the most expensive component of an electric car, and owners want to know their shiny new EV will last as long as the combustion car it replaces.

Battery longevity is particularly important as more used EVs enter the market. Many experts (myself included) have touted pre-owned and off-lease EV deals as a way to bypass the electric-car price premium, but shoppers may be hesitant to roll the dice on higher-mileage vehicles. Many fear a used EV won’t meet their range needs or, worse, could blindside them with an expensive battery replacement.

Ford’s study is another data point that could help allay those worries.

Ford examined more than 36,000 individual vehicles delivered to customers across all 50 US states and Canada during the EV’s first year of sales. A little more than five years later, the automaker says that around 95% of vehicles surveyed retained between 87% and 97% of their battery health (an average of 92%) across the entire 2021 fleet after an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven.

Better battery health means an EV keeps delivering more of its advertised range as the odometer climbs. The 2021 Mustang Mach-E rolled off the assembly line with an EPA-estimated range between 211 and 305 miles, depending on the spec, which means that owners lost around 16 to 24 miles of range over time, according to my back-of-the-napkin math.

That said, there’s no beating the chemistry. Around 2,000 vehicles in the group crossed the 100,000-mile mark, retaining around 91% health. A smaller subset of about 30 drivers reached 200,000 miles in their Mach-Es, with an average battery health of 88%. More miles, it seems, means more wear.

At the extreme anecdotal end of the spectrum, one owner put more than 400,000 miles on his original battery — though Ford didn’t state the specific health of that 2022 Mach-E.

An independent study published by Aviloo earlier this year adds credence to Ford’s reported numbers. An Austrian EV battery diagnostics firm analyzed over 500,000 EVs from 20 global brands to measure battery degradation — at 50,000, 100,000 and 150,000 kilometers — finding that many popular models maintained over 90% battery health at high mileage.

Tesla’s Model Y, which competes directly with the Mach-E, was found to hold around 90.3% battery health at 150,000 kilometers (93,205 miles). Aviloo reported that the Volkswagen ID4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 showed 90.6% and 92.8% retention, respectively, over the same surveyed mileage. The first-generation Nissan Leaf — a much older EV with a smaller battery — showed more degradation at 86.3%, an unfortunate double whammy given its shorter initial range.

According to Ford’s engineers and battery chemists, the Mach-E’s battery was designed to last at least 10 years, adding that the 2021 models in the study use an older nickel-cobalt-manganese, or NCM, chemistry.

Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which will underpin the upcoming Fathom small electric pickup, will use a newer lithium iron phosphate chemistry. That will come with unique charging needs and different battery management calibration than its Class of 2021. The UEV architecture is also built around robust bidirectional charging, so we’ll have to check back in five or so years to see how using your car to power your home affects long-term battery health.

Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.
