#3139. Andy Jassy Just Delivered Great News for Amazon Stock Investors

AWS is growing at its fastest pace in years, and a $578 billion backlog suggests Amazon's huge AI spending is chasing real demand.

Amazon (AMZN +2.94%) has been spending an extraordinary amount of money building artificial intelligence infrastructure, and investors have been waiting to see whether those investments will pay off.

CEO Andy Jassy just gave them a pretty compelling answer.

During Amazon's third-quarter earnings call, Jassy revealed that Amazon Web Services (AWS) is growing faster than it has in nearly five years, with customers consuming new computing capacity almost as quickly as Amazon can install it. "[O]ur plan is working," he said.

That's encouraging news for a company planning to spend approximately $220 billion on capital expenditures this year. There's also plenty more to like about what Jassy had to say.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy. Image source: Amazon.

Amazon's Q3 revenue was $201.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier. Operating income increased 61% to $28.1 billion, giving the company a record operating margin of 13.9%.

AWS was the real standout. The cloud computing business generated $46 billion in revenue, an increase of 39.3% year over year. That's the sixth consecutive quarter of accelerating growth, putting AWS on an annualized revenue run rate of approximately $184 billion.

The business is becoming increasingly profitable. AWS operating income reached $17.8 billion, up 55% from $11.4 billion a year earlier.

Jassy told analysts that AWS has been installing an AI accelerator approximately every 14 seconds. "[C]ustomers are gobbling it up," he said. "Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years."

That's an important distinction. Amazon isn't simply building enormous data centers and hoping customers eventually show up. It's adding capacity to meet existing demand, and the company has the contracts to demonstrate it.

Jassy said AWS ended the quarter with a whopping $578 billion in backlog, representing triple-digit growth from a year earlier. Backlog represents future revenue associated with customer commitments, although the timing of revenue recognition depends on when Amazon delivers the contracted services.

For investors worried that AI infrastructure spending has gotten ahead of demand, that's a meaningful number.

Jassy also said AWS's traditional computing and storage businesses are growing at their fastest rates in several years. So while AI is attracting much of the attention, Amazon's existing cloud services are contributing to the acceleration.

There's another encouraging development. According to Jassy, profitability in AWS's AI business is improving rapidly, even with higher memory costs and depreciation expenses associated with its infrastructure investments.

That matters because Amazon needs more than growing revenue to justify its enormous spending. It needs those investments to generate attractive returns.

Amazon expects approximately $220 billion in capital expenditures during 2026, much of it directed toward AI infrastructure. That's an extraordinary commitment, even for a company of Amazon's size.

The effect is already showing up in its financial statements. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months, compared with positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion a year earlier. The company is generating substantial operating cash flow, but its investments in property and equipment are consuming even more money.

Investors also need to remember that backlog isn't guaranteed profit. Amazon must deliver the computing services, absorb the associated operating expenses, and earn enough to justify its investment.

Jassy believes the demand will support continued expansion. In fact, Amazon projects AWS revenue growth exceeding 40% in both 2027 and 2028. But that's management's expectation, not a guaranteed outcome.

Amazon's Q3 results offer something investors have been demanding from the companies spending heavily on AI: evidence that customers are actually paying for the additional computing power.

AWS revenue is accelerating, operating income is climbing, and its backlog suggests there's substantial demand still waiting to be served.

The company's capital spending remains a legitimate concern, particularly with free cash flow under pressure. A backlog of future business doesn't eliminate the possibility that customers will eventually slow their spending.

But Jassy's comments make a persuasive case that Amazon's AI investments are addressing real demand rather than speculative expectations. For investors willing to accept the near-term spending pressure, that's a compelling reason to remain interested in Amazon stock.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but they're still in a much better place than this time last month.

Mortgage rates are higher today, but only by a little. And they're still hovering below 7%, which is much better than what we saw around this time last month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked up to 6.98% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than Friday and five basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Mortgage rates have more room to rise, as a stronger-than-expected jobs report reinforced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn strong: The October jobs report, released Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Considering Friday’s jobs data, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing, and market sentiment could shift over the next month. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as intended and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates might remain around 7%.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.48% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. #3133. PRA Group: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management expects legal collection costs to peak in 2026 and fall in 2027, a shift that could free up cash for investors weighing PRA's long-term payoff.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, PRA Group (PRAA -1.63%) announced that disciplined cost management helped drive trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA, a measure of cash-oriented operating profit, up 9% year over year. Debt buyers rely on tight expense controls and selective portfolio purchasing to maintain returns across shifting credit cycles. Three key takeaways from management explain how these operational moves position the business for the long term.

Management is prioritizing net returns by redirecting capital away from a competitive U.S. market and toward European debt portfolios. European cash collections exceeded internal expectations by 3% during the quarter, supporting the strategic pivot.

Operational restructuring has eliminated more than 215 corporate roles since October 2025, trimming overhead staffing by over 25%. These workforce reductions cut third-quarter compensation and benefits expenses by 11% year over year, establishing a lower cost base for future operations.

Upfront investments in court-based debt recovery expanded third-quarter U.S. legal cash collections by 19% year over year to $148 million. As teams clear the remaining backlog of accounts, management projects annual legal collection costs will crest in 2026 and decline in 2027, freeing up future cash flow.

Multimarket flexibility allows the business to maintain buying discipline while expanding digital debt recovery capabilities. Deleveraging, or reducing debt relative to earnings, brought net leverage down to 2.6 times earnings for an eighth consecutive quarter.

Cloud infrastructure upgrades and automated workflow tools continue to enhance agent efficiency. Management expects these structural operational changes to compound long-term returns.

#3131. Polestar has a new look with its Formula 2030 concept

The shape looks like a Saab Aero-X, but the nose previews the next Polestar 2.

Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics. But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US, since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress.

The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.)

Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback form factor will go into series production. Successfully packaging the rear seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one.

The nose is a good preview of the next Polestar 2, and the rear light signature will show up on production Polestars. “We wanted to evolve, while respecting, the core design values we demonstrated with previous models that define the Polestar brand in such a recognizable way,” said Nahum Escobedo, head of exterior design at Polestar.

“And with Formula 2030, with its clear Polestar design attributes, like the Dual Blade headlights, wraparound visor-like windshield, and powerful haunches, we have done just that. But we’ve pushed perceptions, preconceptions, and the expected as well, with our considered choices in form language, amplification of the performance topic, and new detailing, like the Single Blade rear lights,” Escobedo said.

Polestar says the four-seat interior pushes its usual minimalism even further. But the end result has avoided the bland fate suffered by the recent Range Rover GT concept, for example. Even though Polestar is committed to developing autonomous driving technology, for manual modes it has added physical controls—rocker switches and rotary controllers, with a user-configurable UI. That’s a new thing for Polestar.

You can’t really tell from the photos, but the Formula 2030 concept explores some sustainability ideas as well. Like BMW’s I Vision Circular, the Formula 2030 was designed using monomaterials and with recycling in mind where possible. The interiors of the doors are fully recyclable, there’s low-emission steel in the chassis, and biocomposites in place of traditional plastics.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#3126. Qualcomm vs. Western Digital: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Qualcomm's chip empire faces a customer concentration question, while Western Digital's storage margins look almost too good to be true.

As mobile connectivity and data storage demands intensify, Qualcomm (QCOM +3.66%) and Western Digital (WDC +9.86%) stand as pivotal players in the tech landscape. Investors must decide which business model offers better potential.

Qualcomm provides the essential chips for smartphones and connected vehicles, while Western Digital manufactures the storage hardware that anchors global data centers. These companies represent different corners of the tech ecosystem, making them an interesting comparison.

Qualcomm is a central figure among semiconductor stocks. It designs the chips that power high-end smartphones and is moving into the automotive and Internet of Things sectors. In its latest annual report, filed in late 2026, the company highlighted key customers like Apple (AAPL +2.43%) and Samsung (SSNLF +0.00%). Since these mobile handset customers account for a large share of sales, customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $43.1 billion, a slight decline of roughly 2.6% from the prior year. Despite the dip in top-line growth, the company reported robust net income of approximately $13.6 billion. This equates to a net margin of close to 31.6%, which is a measure of how much profit is kept from every dollar of sales.

As of Qualcomm's September 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.5. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, with lower ratios indicating a more conservative financial structure. The current ratio, which shows assets available to cover short-term liabilities, stands at nearly 1.9. Free cash flow was close to $8.7 billion for the year, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 31% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Western Digital provides essential data storage solutions using hard disk drive technology for cloud and consumer markets. According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ending in 2026, the company noted a massive reliance on cloud providers. This cloud end market accounted for nearly 89% of revenue in fiscal 2026. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as three individual customers each accounted for 10% or more of total revenue.

For fiscal 2026, revenue reached approximately $12.9 billion, a jump of nearly 35.7% over the previous year. The company delivered net income of close to $9.4 billion. This resulted in an exceptionally high net margin of roughly 72.9%, indicating the company is keeping a large portion of its revenue as profit.

Based on Western Digital's July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1. This indicates a very conservative use of debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at close to 1.3, meaning the company has $1.30 in short-term assets for every $1.00 in short-term debt. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $3.5 billion, and the company maintains a healthy financial position for its future projects.

Qualcomm faces significant revenue concentration in a small number of mobile handset customers. If key customers like Apple transition to their own internally developed solutions, the company could lose a major revenue stream. Additionally, high sales volume in China exposes the business to geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions. Competition is also intense, requiring constant innovation to stay ahead of rivals like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM +3.51%) in manufacturing and other chip designers.

Western Digital is heavily dependent on a limited number of cloud customers and suppliers for critical components. Any disruption in global demand or a shift in technology standards could hurt its market position. The company is currently navigating a transition to new storage technologies like HAMR. Furthermore, macroeconomic volatility and potential product defects or warranty claims represent ongoing concerns for the hardware manufacturer as it competes with companies like Micron Technology (MU +6.25%).

Western Digital appears more attractive based on its forward P/E ratio, while Qualcomm carries a lower P/S ratio relative to its total sales.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I think we've established I am a skeptic with some stocks (even a hater, perhaps). Western Digital has posted impressive growth recently, and yet. The data storage and memory markets are super cyclical, and right now data storage is trading at a wild premium. This long-term chart gives me pause, because WDC was plodding along for ages:

Furthermore, as you can see above, Qualcomm's and Western Digital's long-term returns aren't that far apart. In fact, Western Digital only really ran away with it in the last year or so:

I sometimes buy small positions in spicy, growth-y stocks just to expand my horizons. I don't feel inclined to think Western Digital is attractive in that way. Data and memory storage demand are so closely linked to AI demand right now that I think it's all just toeing the line between a boom and a bubble. Sign me up for boring smartphone chips; Qualcomm gets my vote.

Chase's hotel and resort program, The Edit, gives some cardholders the chance to book stays at spectacular hotels.

The Edit is Chase’s program, and similar to the Fine Hotels & Resorts program from American Express, travelers need to book a prepaid reservation directly through a Chase Travel channel and pay with their Chase card to receive the benefits.

What benefits do you receive when you book through the program? Well, they can be substantial.

The tradeoff of using The Edit program is that it does not necessarily always have the lowest rate. Sometimes you can find a lower rate directly with the hotel or another website. But, when you consider the list of benefits above, any differential in price can more than outweigh the extra cost.

While it belongs to Chase, The Edit is not open to all Chase cardholders. It is a dedicated perk for primary cardholders and authorized users of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® and J.P. Morgan Reserve cards, as well as primary Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders.

Even better is that these eligible Chase cards come with a total of $500 in credits that can be used at The Edit hotels each year. They are divided into two $250 credits that each must be used for at least a two-night stay. And when paying for the rest of your stay through The Edit, cardholders earn 8x Chase Ultimate Rewards® points per dollar spent. In addition, hotel stays booked through The Edit and labeled as “Loyalty Plus” are eligible to also earn points with any associated hotel loyalty program.

These are some of our favorite hotels in the program where you can take advantage of your annual $500 credits as well as earn significant Chase points for a prepaid stay.

Big changes at the hotel include new menus that refocus the restaurant cuisine on modern takes of Chilean recipes. On the top floor, guests can enjoy a panoramic indoor swimming pool beneath a glass atrium, panoramic rooftop terrace and spa offering traditional Andean healing treatments.

Booking a hotel via The Edit leads to instant benefits like free breakfast, property credits, and early check-in and late checkout. While the rates may not always be the lowest you’ll find online, the perks that come with The Edit may more than outweigh any cost differential.

#3123. The New Economics Of Data Center Delay

Francesco Iorio is co-founder and CEO of Augmenta, a company automating building design for the construction industry.

Data center owners and developers are under enormous pressure to bring capacity online quickly. Every month a 60 MW facility sits idle costs its owner an estimated $14.2 million in lost revenue, financing costs and contractual penalties, according to STL Partners’ research.​

Experienced project teams already spend enormous effort identifying schedule exposure and squeezing time from procurement, sequencing, inspections, field execution and other familiar levers. Yet, some of the forces affecting energization remain difficult or impossible to control.​​​

Other forces are within an owner or developer’s control. Late design changes are a good example: Owners may deliberately change requirements to accommodate newer technology such as higher-performance GPUs with different rack, power or cooling requirements, because the economic benefits justify the disruption.​​

The challenge is therefore not always just preventing change, but building a delivery process capable of absorbing disruption.​​

That requires looking beyond the traditional places teams go to recover time. Some parts of the project workflow have historically been treated as relatively fixed because there was little practical ability to accelerate them or make them more responsive.

As technology reaches deeper into design, modeling and coordination, that assumption is beginning to change.​ Rather than replace proven schedule controls, the opportunity is to expand the field of view and to identify where technology has made previously difficult-to-influence parts of the workflow newly actionable.​​​​​​​

Design, building information modeling (BIM) and coordination are examples of areas where technology is beginning to change what is possible.

For instance, AI can now automate time-consuming modeling tasks, generate and evaluate routing options and identify potential conflicts earlier in the coordination process, reducing the manual effort traditionally required to produce and revise complex building designs.​

At Augmenta, where we’re developing spatial AI technology to automate building systems design, we’re seeing firsthand how these capabilities can give skilled practitioners more flexibility to refine designs and respond to project changes. While our work naturally informs my perspective, the broader opportunity extends well beyond any one solution.​

This is particularly relevant in data centers, where owner-driven changes to technology requirements can affect electrical, cooling and other systems. The faster teams can revisit and revise work already completed, the more room they have to accommodate those changes.​​

To identify these opportunities, a useful starting point is to talk to the people performing these workflows. Where is progress constrained by available skilled capacity? Which processes have historically been difficult to accelerate? Where does a change trigger significant downstream rework? And where has technology created options that didn’t exist a few years ago?​​

The answers may reveal constraints that teams previously had to accept but are now worth revisiting, not because they were managed poorly, but because the available tools have changed.​​

Identifying opportunities for acceleration is only part of the equation. Technology only reduces schedule risk if teams can deploy it without introducing greater disruption elsewhere.

The potential impact of any new technology must be balanced against implementation time, integrations, training and change management requirements.​​

This means prioritizing technologies that work within existing processes and give practitioners greater leverage rather than requiring wholesale workflow changes. A tool that accelerates one part of the project but creates additional work or delays elsewhere may simply relocate risk rather than reduce it.​​

To distinguish between the two, teams should start with the specific workflow constraint that a technology addresses and its potential schedule impact. They should also consider the time to value, adoption and training requirements and integration with existing workflows. Equally important is whether the technology can respond to changing project conditions and whether its benefits extend downstream.​​

The goal is to identify technologies that create meaningful flexibility within the delivery process without introducing new constraints that offset the gains.​​

One important consideration is where in the project workflow those gains occur. Not all time savings have the same effect on the overall schedule. Improvements in upstream workflows like design, modeling and coordination can create margin that carries into multiple downstream activities.​​

Accelerating these workflows can create flexibility and optionality later in the schedule, which greatly reduces risk. The value becomes especially apparent when requirements change: time saved upstream gives teams more room to revise, re-coordinate and respond without immediately affecting downstream milestones.​​

I’ve seen this shift firsthand on a large-scale data center project, where an electrical contractor used spatial AI design technology to accelerate the initial modeling process. Rather than spending weeks manually populating the BIM model, the team was able to generate an initial model much faster, freeing skilled virtual design and construction professionals to focus more of their time on reviewing the design, addressing constructibility considerations and preparing for downstream coordination.​

The takeaway goes beyond time saved to how the workflow changes when teams are no longer constrained by the same volume of repetitive manual modeling. That creates additional room to revisit design decisions, coordinate with other trades and accommodate evolving project requirements before they affect downstream activities.​

This is where “speed” becomes a risk-management tool rather than simply a productivity metric.​

Owners and developers cannot eliminate every threat to a data center schedule, nor should they abandon the proven controls they already use to manage risk. ​

But now, there is an opportunity to expand the field of view. As technology reaches deeper into design, modeling, coordination and other parts of the project lifecycle, processes that once offered little room to maneuver may become new sources of schedule margin.​​

By digging deeper into workflows that have historically been difficult to accelerate or influence, teams may find new opportunities to create flexibility before they need it and make the overall schedule more resilient when the inevitable disruption arrives.​​

#3122. Chevron Is Doubling Venezuela Production. ExxonMobil Says It's Not in a Rush. Who's Right?

ExxonMobil may be right to stay out of Venezuela.

Chevron (CVX -0.86%) plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years, potentially more than doubling its oil production there to about 600,000 barrels per day. ExxonMobil (XOM -0.69%), meanwhile, isn't interested in rushing back into Venezuela. And quite frankly, I think ExxonMobil may have the better strategy.

Chevron isn't starting from scratch. The company has operated in Venezuela for more than a century and maintained a presence, even as political instability and economic turmoil have driven other international oil companies away. In fact, in September, Chevron announced agreements providing improved fiscal, commercial, and legal terms for its Venezuelan operations. It also secured additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt.

Management believes it can expand production while keeping total costs below $20 per barrel. Indeed, that's a pretty attractive proposition.

Chevron already has infrastructure, local relationships, and operating experience. Expanding existing production is considerably different from building an entirely new business in a country with Venezuela's history. And if oil prices remain favorable, Chevron could generate substantial additional cash flow without taking on the same level of risk as a newcomer.

Exxon has good reasons to be skeptical. The company has had its Venezuelan assets seized twice, most recently in 2007 under former President Hugo Chávez. CEO Darren Woods has indicated that Exxon would consider returning, but only with stronger legal protections and investment terms that justify the risks. I don't blame him.

Venezuela's oil infrastructure needs substantial investment, political uncertainty remains high, and there's no guarantee future governments will honor today's agreements. And there's also reason to consider long-term oil demand.

There are varying projections on this. The IEA projects that global oil demand could plateau around 2030. Wood Mackenzie has that plateau hitting in 2032. TotalEnergies (TTE +0.20%) has it between 2035 and 2040, while OPEC suggests "robust global oil demand growth prospects to 2050, with no signs of oil demand peaking over the forecast period." But even with OPEC's optimistic scenario, 2050 is only about 23 years away.

Of course, even if demand levels off, existing oil fields will continue declining. The industry will still need replacement production. But if demand growth slows while producers keep expanding capacity, oil prices could face additional pressure. Under these conditions, spending billions on politically risky projects becomes harder to justify.

Chevron's expansion isn't necessarily a mistake. Its existing operations, relatively low production costs, and improved contractual terms could make Venezuela a profitable source of additional oil production. But ExxonMobil doesn't have the same advantages. It would potentially need to commit substantial capital to rebuild operations in a country that has already confiscated its assets.

The company has other places to invest, including Guyana and the Permian Basin, where it has established operations and greater confidence in its ability to generate returns. Overall, ExxonMobil's strategy just makes sense. Yes, Chevron could make plenty of money in Venezuela. But ExxonMobil is demonstrating that having the financial resources to pursue an opportunity doesn't mean you should. Sometimes the better investment decision is knowing when to walk away.

#3120. ​The Two-Headed Hydra: How AI Is Changing Software Development And Cyber Risk

Ken Ammon is CEO of CodeHunter, a serial entrepreneur who exited OPĀQ and NetSec, and former U.S. Air Force captain at the NSA.

​It sounds like a security nightmare, but it is quickly becoming operational reality: The same AI capabilities helping enterprises build software faster now help adversaries attack it faster.

AI coding tools and development agents are now part of the software delivery process. They help developers write scripts, update dependencies, troubleshoot builds, generate tests and move code through workflows with less manual effort. Attackers are using the same class of capabilities to build malicious software more efficiently.

They can automate reconnaissance, generate exploit code, test evasive variations and tailor malware to a target environment with ease. AI is now accelerating enterprise software development and software-based attacks at the same time.

Meanwhile, AI-driven malware undermines the signals security teams have historically used to make trust decisions. Source, signing, provenance, dependency scans and reputation remain important, but become unreliable when attack code has never been seen before, is short-lived and designed to change.

These indicators do not prove what code will do when it runs. Post-execution detection has the same limitation with worse timing. By the time suspicious behavior is visible, the artifact may already have accessed credentials, modified system settings or established persistence.

The more durable signal is behavior, and the most important decision point is whether that behavior should be allowed before execution.

​We are already seeing why. Recent npm supply chain campaigns show how quickly malicious packages can move into developer environments and CI/CD workflows. Some packages are designed to steal cloud and build credentials. Others profile developer machines or abuse dependency confusion to blend into normal package resolution. The attack path is familiar to any security team: A package looks useful, gets pulled into a workflow, runs during installation or build and inherits the permissions of the environment that executed it.

​AI raises the pressure on traditional security models because it reduces the cost of variation. Attackers can generate more package names, alter payloads, test different install behaviors and adapt code faster than a team can manually review each artifact.

​The same dynamic applies inside the enterprise. AI coding tools and development agents can generate scripts, modify files, recommend dependencies and issue commands as part of normal software workflows. In many cases, a human still approves the pull request or reviews the output. In other cases, the review is shallow because the pipeline is moving fast and the AI-produced change looks routine.

​That is where the risk concentrates. A generated script may complete the requested task while also introducing access the organization did not intend. A dependency update may solve a build issue while bringing in a package with dangerous install-time behavior. A container may pass through a pipeline while carrying logic that should never run in production. The issue is not whether the code was created by an employee, an AI assistant or an attacker. The issue is what the code is capable of doing when it executes.

​The form of an attack can keep changing while its objective stays the same. A package may be renamed, a payload may produce a new hash, and a script may be rewritten each time a model is prompted. But code still has to act to achieve its purpose. If the goal is credential theft, persistence, external communication or unauthorized system change, those behaviors eventually have to show up. That is why security teams need the ability to make an enforceable decision before execution.

​The goal is not to slow development by forcing manual review of every artifact, but to identify where code gains meaningful execution rights and put an enforceable decision point in front of those paths before it runs.

​A good starting point is developer workstations, CI/CD runners, package managers, build identities, deployment scripts, container promotion paths and automation jobs. This is where code often inherits trust from the person, tool or service account that launched it. A package running on a developer laptop is one level of risk. A package running in a build system with access to signing keys, cloud credentials or production deployment rights has a much bigger security blast radius.

​The control point should focus on behavior before execution. If an artifact is about to run in a sensitive environment, the organization should know what it is capable of doing. Will it attempt to access secrets, create persistence or make unauthorized system changes? When the behavior falls outside policy, code execution should be prevented, restricted, isolated or the artifact sent for review before it is allowed to run.

​This approach is not new. Zero trust is already used to assess users, devices, sessions and workloads before access is granted. By moving the trust decision closer to execution, we can apply the same discipline to code.

VA mortgage borrowers are quietly navigating a knowledge gap. Here’s how to close it.

If your understanding of a VA home loan starts and ends with “it’s for the military,” you’re not alone. For many eligible veterans and service members, the intricate workings (and benefits) of this U.S. government-backed mortgage are obscured behind lackluster guidance.

While there are classes and resources available, the military is broadly wary of steering members in a specific direction, says Alex Rodino, a real estate agent and U.S. Army veteran who served 10 years as an infantry officer and military advisor. “A lot of the course material is just very generic,” he says.

And that’s not a surprise. Considering the sheer size and scope of the military, providing personalized advice on VA loans to all its members would be no easy task.

That leaves real estate agents and lenders as the last line of defense, which is where a big part of the knowledge gap exists. Rodino purchased his first home in 2020 with a VA loan and says he didn’t like how ignorant he felt during the process.

“The reason I actually got my real estate license to begin with was because of that experience I had,” Rodino says. “Looking back on it, I had a lot of questions that didn't really get answered.”

But how can VA borrowers navigate this knowledge gap without having to become mortgage experts in their spare time? Here are some of the most important things to know when considering a VA loan, according to the financial experts and borrowers who have lived it.

“My mortgage broker said, hey, you might qualify for this, look it up,” says Elizabeth Valente, a real estate investor and former U.S. Army officer who bought her first home using a VA loan in 2021. When it came to the application process, she felt crucial information wasn’t readily available to her or fully explained.

In hindsight, Valente says, working with an agent or lender who had detailed VA loan experience would have been beneficial. Not only would it help untangle the specific paperwork and appraisal requirements, but that expertise offers an important layer of support for military borrowers.

“For some processes in the military, it's very hand-holding,” Valente says. “I'll tell you what to wear, what to bring, when to be there.” But that’s not always true when transitioning back to civilian life, and parsing specifics of a loan process can be challenging. “I don't think a typical Realtor would understand what that person's going through,” Valente says.

Finding professionals with the right expertise involves asking questions — and lots of them.

“If I'm the smartest person in the room, we have an issue,” Valente says. “Don't be afraid to tell someone if something doesn't make sense or if you don't understand the numbers.”

Before agreeing to work with a lender or mortgage broker, ask how their process works, what companies they work with, and how familiar they are with VA loans. Treat the initial conversation like an interview — you’re hiring them, not the other way around.

Knowing where to find your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and how much you might be eligible to borrow is the responsibility of the person applying, Valente says. “All that information — it is available in the [VA] website but you really have to dig for it.”

And this information isn’t recreational reading — your COE lists your "basic entitlement," which is a crucial figure in VA lending. If you have full basic entitlement, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) generally guarantees 25% of the loan, which in most cases lets you put 0% down.

Why? With a quarter of the loan guaranteed by the VA, the lender is more protected and thus more willing to forgo a down payment.

So how do you know if you have full basic entitlement? Look for the figure $36,000 on your COE. This dollar amount represents full entitlement. Technically, basic entitlement is for loans up to $144,000, but then your bonus entitlement kicks in and you can go higher. The VA doesn’t set loan limits when you have full entitlement — though your lender will still decide how much you can borrow based on your income, debts, credit and the home’s appraised value.

Let’s say you want to buy a home in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and you need a $200,000 loan. In order to put no money down, your entitlement needs to cover at least 25% of the loan amount — in this example, that’s $50,000. After you purchase the home, your COE will show your basic entitlement as $0 and the entitlement charged to a previous loan as $50,000.

“Serving in the military is a unique investing opportunity that most people don't get,” Rodino says. “I wish someone had told me to buy a house when I got to my first duty station.”

If he’d known it was possible or understood how, Rodino says he would have been able to buy in 2017, move in 2020, rent out his first home and then repeat the process. “I'd have three by now and the first one would probably be paid off.”

This particular plan is partly based on the unique schedule of many military members. “Generally, you're moving anywhere from two to four to six years,” Rodino says. Owning multiple properties also leverages two big (and often misunderstood) perks of the VA loan: It’s possible to have more than one active loan at the same time, and after one year, you may be able to convert your primary residence to a rental.

Let’s go back to Fayetteville, North Carolina. After two years, you decide to rent out the home because you’re moving to Bell County, Texas. The home you want to buy in Bell County is $300,000, and in order to make no down payment, you need the VA to guarantee 25% of the loan ($75,000).

Because you no longer have full basic entitlement — remember, you already have an active VA loan elsewhere — your entitlement is capped at 25% of the conforming loan limit in the county where you plan to buy, minus what’s already being used on your first loan ($50,000 in our Fayetteville example).

Now for the math: The current conforming loan limit in Bell County is $832,750. Multiply this figure by 25% and subtract the $50,000 already in use: You have $158,187.50 of entitlement available to you — plenty to guarantee the $75,000 needed on the new loan.

If all of this sounds overwhelming, you’re not wrong. There are resources out there to help you figure all of this out, Rodino says. “The problem is, they're not always practical or they're not always apparent.”

The VA has a website that can walk you through entitlement calculations, but you should also ask your lender, broker or agent. If you’re working with experienced folks, they’ll be able to explain these details and help you get the most out of the VA’s guarantees.

The key takeaway is this: While each VA loan must initially be for a primary residence, borrowers can leverage their entitlement to build an investment portfolio without needing to cough up large down payments.

But these examples don’t consider all of the factors that go into approvals. Like most mortgages, your income, debts and assets dictate your eligibility. And although the VA doesn’t impose credit score minimums, most lenders do — NerdWallet's analysis shows 620 is a common floor.

It’s also important to note that a VA loan’s 0% down isn’t free. VA loans carry a funding fee based on how much you’re putting down and whether it’s your first or subsequent use (certain disabled veterans are exempt). You can pay this up front at closing or roll it into the loan amount; again, your team of professionals should be able to walk you through your options.

“I think there's the assumption that this is what we do: We get our VA home loan and we go buy a home,” says Julie Soares, financial readiness director for the Wounded Warrior Project. When we’re given access to a benefit that offers discounts and perks, it can be hard not to take advantage of it. But this is why financial awareness is critical.

There are a lot of conversations happening right now around homeownership and whether it’s the right choice, especially as affordability remains challenging. So if you haven’t heard it recently, here’s a reminder: Buying property is not the only way to build wealth or create financial security.

“The financial readiness program at Wounded Warrior Project is really leaning into getting further upstream in those conversations,” Soares says. Having a clear understanding of your benefits before you need to use them allows you to make more informed choices.

While it's helpful to understand your entitlement and what you may be eligible to borrow, you don't have to know every little detail about mortgages, or navigate the process alone. Sometimes, the most important thing to know about VA loans is where to turn for help.

If you are unsure of your eligibility or want more information about home loans, you can call the VA's home loans hotline at 877-827-3702.

“Please reach out to Wounded Warrior Project, reach out to the VA, reach out to any service organization,” Soares says. “Not one organization is gonna be able to fix or solve all of these problems. We have to do this as a group.”

#3117. 1 Overlooked Dividend Stock With a 54-Year Winning Streak Worth Buying Now

PepsiCo has raised dividends annually for decades.

It's not often that a stock that consistently raises dividends trades at a discount. But that's the case with PepsiCo (PEP +0.38%).

Despite the company's long dividend history, investors have been dismayed by the company's recent earnings. However, that creates a buying opportunity for investors looking for steadily rising dividends and potential capital appreciation.

Here's a closer examination of why PepsiCo's dividend-raising streak doesn't look likely to end anytime soon.

PepsiCo's dividend-raising streak has reached 54 years. There's a special group for companies that have increased payments for at least 50 straight years: Dividend Kings.

The board of directors hasn't been approving nominal, small increases, either. PepsiCo raised June's payout by 4% to $1.48 per share. This latest boost looks sustainable, based on the company's earnings. PepsiCo's payout ratio, or dividends compared to earnings, is 73%.

The shares also have a much higher dividend yield than the overall stock market, as measured by the S&P 500 index, which investors often use as a proxy for large-cap stocks. PepsiCo's stock yields 4.2% versus 1.1% for the index.

Consistently increasing dividends, secure payments, and a higher-than-market dividend yield sound good. Yet investors haven't been impressed with PepsiCo's results. This year, through Nov. 6, the share price dove 1.5%, vastly underperforming the S&P 500's 7.8% gain.

The company has struggled with product volume for a while due to a tough economic environment and competitive pressures. There has been some progress on that front, but it's been uneven.

Its fiscal third-quarter revenue (ended Sept. 5), adjusted to remove foreign-currency translation and acquisitions/divestitures, grew 3.1% year over year. However, higher volume only contributed 0.5 percentage points. Also, cost pressures weighed on the bottom line, with adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increasing just 1.5%.

For the year, management now expects EPS to grow 1% to 2%. That's down from its previous guidance of 4% to 6%.

However, PepsiCo should recoup higher costs over time. Notably, management has been focusing on product innovation to win back customers, add volume, and expand the company's margin. These changes take time, though. However, it's positive that the company is taking steps to adjust to consumer tastes.

Aside from the benefits of higher dividends and an attractive yield, the shares appear well-valued. The stock has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 18 compared to the 10-year median of 26. It also has a lower valuation than the S&P 500, which has a P/E multiple of 25.

The multiple should expand over time as PepsiCo's sales and earnings growth pick up. That creates a powerful opportunity to collect dividends and potentially produce outsize stock gains.

#3115. ServiceNow vs. Snowflake: Which Tech Stock Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Both software leaders are growing fast, but one is weighed down by fears of AI disruption and the other by a steep price tag.

Should you invest in the operational brain of the modern office or the central engine of its data? We look at ServiceNow (NOW +0.78%) and Snowflake (SNOW +5.53%) to see which is the better buy.

ServiceNow specializes in automating workflows and digitizing business processes, making life easier for employees. Snowflake provides a cloud-native platform for storing, sharing, and analyzing massive amounts of data. Both companies are high-growth leaders in their respective categories, but they follow very different business models and possess distinct financial profiles.

ServiceNow operates an AI platform that connects people and processes by automating manual tasks across departments such as IT, HR, and customer service. The company serves roughly 8,700 enterprise customers, including more than 600 clients that generate over $5 million in annual contract value. It has expanded its reach through strategic alliances with major tech companies.

On a trailing-12-month basis through the September quarter, revenue reached nearly $15.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 22% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company remains consistently profitable, reporting net income of close to $1.4 billion for the period. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 9.4%, demonstrating the ability to generate significant earnings while continuing to invest in its global expansion and AI integration.

As of its September 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.6x, indicating that its total debt is low relative to its shareholders' equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term bills, is roughly 0.7x.

TTM free cash flow was roughly $4.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 35.9% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Snowflake provides the AI Data Cloud, a platform that allows organizations to break down data silos and collaborate across multiple cloud environments. The company has grown its customer base to over 13,328 accounts, including nearly 800 of the Forbes Global 2000. It relies on a deep network of partners, including global systems integrators such as Accenture and Infosys, to help customers implement and scale their data strategies.

TTM revenue through Snowflake's July quarter reached nearly $5.4 billion, a growth rate of approximately 32% year over year. Despite this rapid top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of close to $1.1 billion over the same period. This resulted in a net margin of roughly -20%, as the business continues to prioritize customer acquisition and product development over immediate GAAP profitability.

As of its July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 1.3x, calculated by dividing total debt by shareholders' equity. Its current ratio is approximately 0.9x, providing a healthy cushion to meet short-term obligations.

TTM free cash flow through July was nearly $1.2 billion, but note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 130.9% of operating cash flow, meaning this non-cash add-back heavily inflates cash generation.

ServiceNow faces intense competition from legacy and AI-native vendors, including Salesforce and Oracle, which may put pressure on pricing. The company also addresses the complexities of integrating AI technology while maintaining high levels of data security.

Furthermore, ServiceNow navigates significant government contracting hurdles and the constant challenge of attracting and retaining highly skilled AI talent in a tight labor market.

Snowflake faces significant competitive pressure from large public cloud providers, such as Alphabet and Microsoft, that both host its platform and offer competing data tools. Its consumption-based revenue model introduces volatility, making it difficult for investors to forecast quarterly results with precision.

ServiceNow appears significantly more affordable on a price basis, trading at a much lower multiple for both its sales and future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

In this comparison, the Forward P/E compares the share price to future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio compares market cap to sales over the past twelve months.

Both companies have steadily grown revenue at high rates, despite competition in their respective market. However, I would buy ServiceNow for a few reasons.

ServiceNow stock is down over worries that agentic AI tools will reduce demand for its software. But subscription revenue growth has remained fairly steady throughout 2026, and management's guidance calls for 21% year-over-year growth in constant currency for the full year.

It appears to have a successful path to positioning itself as the crucial governance and security layer for agentic AI. Its backlog grew 21% year-over-year last quarter, indicating demand for its offering remains strong.

Snowflake is also remaining resilient despite concerns about competition in its market. But I prefer to buy ServiceNow because of its lower valuation. Snowflake trades at high multiples of earnings and sales, while ServiceNow trades at a more average multiple of forward earnings despite above-average revenue growth and margins. I believe ServiceNow is likely undervalued and can outperform the market, possibly in 2027 and in the coming years.

#3114. How Reading The Room Can Help Prevent ERP Go-Live Delays

Komal Goyal is CEO of 6e Technologies, a global IT advisory firm specializing in ERP implementation for commercial and government clients.

​Should a date decide when an ERP system is ready to go live?

ERP go-live dates are often tied to hard-to-move commitments, such as a fiscal year-end or a merger and acquisition (M&A) event. As the date approaches, teams focus on what dashboards can measure: testing, defects, integrations and training. But those measures do not capture every readiness risk.

Take Rhode Island’s payroll as an example. It went live as planned. Within weeks, unions reported missing wages, unpaid overtime and incorrect deductions. Root causes await an independent review, but the vendor cited the complexity of moving from fragmented legacy systems to a unified platform. However, technology rarely fails on its own; how people adopt, use and work around it often shapes the outcome.

Across more than 30 successful ERP implementations, I have found readiness gaps often appear first in behavior. Reading those cues early allows time to address problems while protecting the go-live date.

This is an important principle of ERP implementation assurance: independently testing whether an organization is ready to operate a new system, rather than relying solely on whether an implementation is on schedule.​

Reading the room starts with signals that never appear in test results or sign-offs. Here are five I watch for:

I have been left guessing in requirements discussions because only part of a process was shared. That under-sharing may be oversight or reluctance to expose informal work-arounds. Either way, missed details become missed requirements, which often surface after go-live as defects, delays or operational problems.

When a stakeholder stops discussing the future-state process to defend the current one, I pay attention. The objection may be valid or reflect concerns about changing responsibilities, authority or job security. I have seen people make a process sound more complex than it is or insist the new system cannot support it.​

Left unread, that defensiveness can lead to customizing around a problem that may not exist, adding effort and risk until go-live slips.

If a user engaged in testing suddenly gets frustrated, it’s easy to assume that perhaps the workflow is clunkier or a feature they rely on is missing. But sometimes the “missing feature” is lost authority, because a step they considered critical is no longer needed.​

If that goes unread, they may disengage from testing, and issues they would have caught surface later on.

Silence is harder to read. When someone who used to speak up goes quiet, I want to know what changed. They may feel speaking up is pointless, or fear what it could cost them. The concerns people stop raising do not disappear. They arrive at go-live.

Every go-live has a list of items to fix later. The list itself is not the warning sign; it is how difficult issues are handled. I pay attention when a question makes the room uneasy and is quickly deferred until after go-live without a clear owner or plan.​

Sometimes, a failed test is dismissed as minor because the launch date is approaching. Without assessing how it could affect daily operations, the team risks discovering the consequences after launch, when resolving them may be more disruptive.

Recognizing these patterns gives teams a chance to act early.​

I’ve seen readiness issues get harder to fix once go-live pressure builds. That’s why a strong change management lead should work closely with stakeholders to act on these findings in time.

However, more time does not inherently solve the problem. Idaho’s Luma rollout was delayed twice, yet an independent review found its change management left agencies and employees underprepared to work differently.

When a cue surfaces, look beyond the behavior to its cause.

If details are withheld, broaden the conversation until the full process, including informal work-arounds, is clear. If someone defends the old process or reports missing functionality, determine what need lies behind the objection before customizing or deferring a solution. If a workflow feels harder, assess whether the issue is design or user capability, then provide the necessary changes, training or support.

Where authority is changing, clarify decision rights. Retire work-arounds only when the new system meets the needs they served. If users go quiet, speak with them privately to understand why, then explain what concerns were addressed and what remains unresolved.​​

​​Importantly, while a change lead can drive this work, appointing someone outside of the program to independently challenge whether people are ready can help to make sure the pressure to meet the deadline does not overshadow unresolved readiness risks.​

As go-live nears, deadline pressure takes over. System integrators focus on delivery, internal teams manage execution, and leaders balance competing business priorities. Generative AI can accelerate this push, cutting implementation effort by up to 40% and testing time by 70%.

But faster delivery does not answer whether the organization is ready. That question needs someone far enough from delivery to challenge readiness. A dashboard or even GenAI can show participation dropped, but rarely why a respected user went quiet. Here, human judgment still has the edge over AI.

Emotional intelligence helps read that cue, and ERP experience tells whether it’s ordinary friction or a real readiness risk. Having the strategy in place to say “not yet” is how the date stops deciding the system change.​​

#3112. First Look: Inside United’s New Club at Washington Dulles

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The airline’s newest lounge will be the second-largest in the network, offering flyers an upgraded experience at Dulles.

You’ll no longer have to go to the basement to get into a United Club at Washington Dulles International Airport.

The brand-new United Club in the new IAD Concourse E spans nearly 40,000 square feet across an upstairs floor and can seat 630 passengers, making it a significant upgrade to the carrier’s existing lounge portfolio at the airport. It’s the second-largest United Club after its newest lounge in Houston, which opened just weeks earlier.

The new lounge by gates E14 and E16 opens to customers Nov. 10, 2026. United invited me to a media preview of the lounge, and here’s what you can expect inside.

The lounge features several nods to D.C.’s iconic landmarks and monuments, as well as the region’s natural beauty.

When you first enter the lounge, you’ll need to scan your boarding pass and then head up the escalators (stairs and elevators are also available) to get to the lounge.

One of my favorite design features as a former D.C. resident is that escalator ride up, which has been recreated to feel like you’re inside a Metro station.

Thankfully, the escalator ride is not as long as at some stations. Looking at you, Dupont Circle!

Once you're upstairs, you’ll walk into the heart of the lounge, with two buffet stations, a centerpiece bar and plenty of seating options, whether you’re traveling as a group or by yourself. (More on food and beverage options later.)

It’s impossible to miss the soaring ceilings in this lounge, especially compared to the bunker-like atmosphere at some of the existing United Clubs.

Don’t forget to look up, where you’ll see a cherry blossom sculpture, an homage to one of the region’s most popular attractions.

There are also two additional lounging areas on both sides of the central area. One is inspired by the Blue Ridge Mountains, which you can see in the distance.

The other has a cherry blossom theme, with light fixtures that branch out from the ceiling.

Massive windows run throughout the lounge, allowing in tons of natural light and offering fantastic views of the airfield. United has a major presence at IAD, so expect to see plenty of United planes.

The United Club has a full kitchen, allowing it to offer upgraded food options compared to its existing lounges at IAD.

You can expect to find sandwiches, salads and hot protein dishes. The lounge also had a ramen bar and a chili bar set up during my visit.

The two buffet stations are located right next to each other, with a dessert station in between.

If you want something to drink, you can head to the bar or one of the hydration stations throughout the space.

There’s plenty of seating at the bar, which has a double archway design. There are also large TVs if you’re trying to keep up with one of Washington’s many sports teams.

The United Club has eight phone booths for those who need to make a call. They’re split between the two lounging areas in the club.

You'll also find a single-stall private restroom, a wellness room, and dedicated men’s and women’s restrooms.

There are no showers in this lounge. To access a shower in a United lounge, you’ll need to head to the Polaris Lounge, reserved exclusively for eligible business class passengers flying on United and select partner airlines.

You can access the United Club by holding elite status, a lounge membership, the right credit card or an eligible premium cabin ticket.

If there’s availability, United sells day passes at the door for flights departing within three hours. You’ll also need a valid same-day boarding pass on a United or Star Alliance flight.

Holding the right credit card is probably the easiest way to get in. United’s most high-end card comes with a United Club membership, while others might offer one-time passes.

If you’re looking for a United lounge, the newest club in Concourse E is where you want to be. It offers more space, lots of light and elevated food options compared to other United Clubs.

Its massive footprint could also ease overcrowding, a common complaint with other lounges.

One thing to consider is location. The concourses at IAD are spread out, and you may need to take a mobile lounge or train to get there. If you want to check out the lounge, make sure you give yourself enough time to get to your gate.

#3111. Anthropic Just Took a Big Step Toward Its Public Debut. Here's What You Need to Know.

The Claude developer finally set a price range for its IPO, and it's lower than many investors expected.

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude family of AI models, has been one of the most anticipated IPOs in years. There has been speculation that it could break records set earlier this year by SpaceX (SPCX +5.81%) for valuation, the amount of money raised in the offering, or both.

Investors finally got some of the details they've been waiting for. Anthropic's latest draft prospectus indicates that the company and some of its existing investors plan to sell 825 million shares at a range of $70 to $78 per share.

Here's what the price range tells us about Anthropic's valuation, when the stock could start trading, and what else it means for investors.

At $70 to $78 a share, the IPO would raise $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion. It's worth noting that not all of that money goes to Anthropic, as 23.65 million shares (roughly 3% of the total) are being sold by existing shareholders.

Anthropic also lined up a separate $26 billion private placement with seven tech heavyweights, including Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%), Alphabet's (GOOGL +1.18%) Google, Microsoft (MSFT +2.75%), and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +3.51%). Including the placement, Anthropic could bring in as much as $90.4 billion. This would surpass the roughly $85.7 billion SpaceX raised.

It's also worth noting that this range is already a revision. A day earlier, a version of the filing sent to bankers showed about 867 million shares at $70 to $80.

Plus, underwriters will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million additional shares, which could add nearly $10 billion to the amount raised, based on the high end of the price range.

Based on about 16.9 billion fully diluted shares implied by Anthropic's amended filing, the range works out to roughly $1.19 trillion to $1.32 trillion. Once you add the new IPO shares and the shares going to the cornerstone investors, my estimate rises to about $1.27 trillion to $1.41 trillion.

For context, Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its private funding round in May, so the IPO range is about 32% to 46% higher. But it's well below the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation reported by The Wall Street Journal in October, before the tech sell-off that followed the midterm elections cooled investors' appetite. SpaceX's IPO valued that company at more than $1.7 trillion, so as things stand now, Anthropic isn't likely to set a new valuation record.

One thing we can do after the latest version of Anthropic's S-1 is to start calculating some valuation metrics to help determine how cheap or expensive the stock could be.

The price-to-sales (P/S) ratio compares a company's market value with its revenue, and it's one of the most useful yardsticks for a company that isn't consistently profitable yet. Anthropic generated $17.0 billion of revenue in the third quarter, up 47% from the second quarter. Annualize that, and you get about $68 billion, which puts Anthropic at roughly 19 to 21 times sales at the IPO range.

That's expensive by most standards, but not outrageous for a company growing this fast. Anthropic's revenue in the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion, up from $1.2 billion in the same period a year earlier. If it keeps growing anywhere near that pace, today's multiple will look much lower in hindsight.

Of course, growth like this rarely lasts. Anthropic also swung back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, after reporting its first operating profit in the second quarter.

Anthropic's roadshow, the series of meetings where management pitches the stock to big institutional investors, is underway this week. Shares could start trading on the Nasdaq as soon as late next week, according to multiple sources.

We don't know the exact date yet. But companies usually publish a price range when the roadshow begins, roughly one to two weeks before the IPO prices. The final price is generally set the evening before the first trade, and it can come in above, within, or below the range, depending on demand. Anthropic has already trimmed its range once, so I wouldn't treat $70-$78 as final.

A few other things stand out to me. The cornerstone investors are also among Anthropic's largest suppliers and partners, signaling confidence in the company but potentially deepening conflicts of interest. Anthropic's IPO will also be the first major test of AI valuations since the recent tech sell-off, so its reception could set the tone for other AI companies hoping to go public. And Alphabet and Amazon (AMZN +2.94%) both already own stakes in Anthropic, which will soon have a public market price.

Having said all that, the price range gives investors something concrete to evaluate for the first time. At roughly 20 times annualized sales, Anthropic isn't cheap, but its valuation is more reasonable than the $2 trillion figure that was floating around just a few weeks ago.

It's also worth noting that the actual IPO price doesn't necessarily have to fall in this range, especially if interest is high. It's not uncommon for popular IPOs to end up pricing shares above the high end of the stated range.

While AMD shares have jumped 137% in 2026, Intel has clocked respectable gains of 60% as of this writing. We will examine AMD's and Intel's latest results and determine which of these two chipmakers is the better buy right now.

Intel's revenue from its data center and AI (DCAI) segment increased by 78% year over year in Q3 to $7.3 billion. What's worth noting is that the company's DCAI revenue growth has been accelerating in recent quarters.

Looking ahead, AMD expects stronger growth in data centers, driven by the increasing adoption of its latest MI455X graphics cards, which it has begun shipping in volume to customers, as well as its Epyc server CPUs. AMD CEO Lisa Su remarked on the latest earnings call:

#3107. The Biggest AI Agent Risk Is The Workaround Nobody Approved

Enterprises are learning that approving an AI agent and its intended task does not guarantee a secure outcome. How the agent completes the work is proving to be one of the biggest AI visibility and security gaps in the modern enterprise.

OpenAI’s review of unexpected model behavior during training and evaluation has now led it to notify more than 100 organizations. Its earlier disclosures showed how agents could depart from intended methods while pursuing a task. Models uploaded files to public services, communicated across separate training samples and searched public repositories for leaked API keys. In one case, collaborating agents made a workbook publicly downloadable after the intended local handoff failed. Similar behavior was also evident in the Hugging Face incident, where agents found workarounds when they encountered resistance.

That these incidents occurred in testing environments under close observation makes the enterprise lesson more urgent. If agents can find unauthorized routes in a lab designed to study their behavior, organizations should assume similar behaviors will surface in production environments where the execution path is harder to observe.

The common pattern is persistence. When one route fails, the agent uses the access, tools or communication channels still available to finish the task. The problem arises when the actions taken are not authorized.

That path can also be hijacked rather than chosen. In prompt-injection scenarios, malicious instructions embedded in a file can steer an agent to move data through an approved service, even when the sandbox operates as designed. The final output may look legitimate while the route to it has been compromised.

For security teams, this means that oversight must extend beyond the prompt and the final output.

Security teams already collect much of the evidence they need. The difficulty is seeing how it fits together.

An agent may receive an instruction in one application, continue through an employee’s authenticated session and hand part of the work to another agent. The prompt, subsequent actions and handoff are recorded in different places, leaving no clear record of how the original request became the final outcome.

Identity, endpoint and application tools record individual events, but investigators are left to reconstruct the execution path connecting them.

This also makes attribution difficult. Activity performed by an employee and activity performed by an agent can appear under the same identity. Investigators may know who owns the account but still be unable to determine who or what launched a process, handled a file or made an external connection.

Viewed alone, each event may appear routine. The risk shows up in the order of events, particularly when an agent encounters resistance and changes course. If that sequence is lost, security teams cannot tell whether the agent remained within the authority it was given. They may see a file transfer without seeing the failed attempt that prompted it or know that a task succeeded without knowing that the agent changed the destination.

​Organizations need a continuous record linking the person who initiated the task with the agent’s activity and the data affected. That record must follow the work across systems and show when the agent changes its approach.

Permissions still define where an agent can operate. They cannot demonstrate that every subsequent action remains appropriate. When an agent moves sensitive information outside an approved location or reaches beyond the task’s established purpose, the organization needs enough context to recognize the change and intervene.

That also means defining what an agent should do when an approved route fails. Some alternatives may be acceptable within the task’s existing authority. A workaround that changes who can access sensitive data should require approval before the agent proceeds.

This changes approval from a single decision into an ongoing assessment. The organization defines the agent’s authority before work begins, then evaluates whether its behavior remains consistent with that authority.

As agents gain more discretion, security teams will need to examine the path between instruction and outcome. The immediate risk is not an agent refusing its task but completing it through actions the organization never approved.

#3106. Prediction Markets Are Arriving in Your Investing App, and That Makes Us Nervous

Its articles, interactive tools and other content are provided to you for free, as self-help tools and for informational purposes only. They are not intended to provide investment advice. Examples are hypothetical, and we encourage you to seek personalized advice from qualified professionals regarding specific investment issues.
