We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. And while our site doesn’t feature every company or financial product available on the market, we’re proud that the guidance we offer, the information we provide and the tools we create are objective, independent, straightforward — and free.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us. This may influence which products we review and write about (and where those products appear on the site), but it in no way affects our recommendations or advice, which are grounded in thousands of hours of research. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews of their products or services. Here is a list of our partners.

Prediction markets are booming, but that doesn’t make them a sound investment strategy.

The investing information provided on this page is for educational purposes only. NerdWallet, Inc. does not offer advisory or brokerage services, nor does it recommend or advise investors to buy or sell particular stocks, securities or other investments.

Around this time every year, we conduct NerdWallet’s annual broker review process. We assess what’s changed in the industry, discuss which brokerage features matter most (and which ones now matter less), and finally, we do the work by opening accounts to test them.

Prediction markets, which have made their way into some of the most popular investing apps, came up more than we expected in testing this year.

At first, we decided to simply collect information on who does and doesn’t offer access to them, without intending to reward or penalize a broker either way. It would be a neutral presentation of facts, not something that would factor into how we scored a broker.

But one afternoon, all together in the office, we confronted an uncomfortable question: “Do prediction markets, and such easy access to them within an investment app, go against NerdWallet’s editorial house views?”

After careful consideration, we all agreed: they do.

So we started to configure our 2027 rubric with a firmer stance against this trendy feature, penalizing brokers that actively market sports and entertainment event contracts, and whose prediction markets come with few, if any, guardrails.

We’ve distilled our discussion down to three main points:

These products are being marketed alongside investments.

We fear they could be discouraging long-term investing.

Let’s start here: Many aspects of trading could be seen as gambling-adjacent. Options, futures, highly leveraged single-day equity bets and even crypto can all easily fall into the “highly speculative” category. So why are we picking on prediction markets in particular?

In our view, a key differentiator is a much lower barrier to entry with few in-app guardrails in place.

Most of the products we mentioned above require some level of fluency — and at times even permission from the broker — to dabble in. To trade options, for example, you need to answer questions about your investing proficiency, your finances and more. And even after approval, the terminology required to trade can be so intimidating that the language itself can become an indirect deterrent.

Event contracts, which form the backbone of prediction markets, are largely presented in the vernacular, and our testing showed approval to trade them is completed with a few taps from the home screen. Moreover, their content is often unrelated to finance — according to a May 2026 report by the Pew Research Center, around 80% of volume on the prediction market platform Kalshi was for sports events[1]Pew Research Center. Trading Volume on Prediction Markets Has Soared in Recent Months. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

Answering a binary question (yes/no; this/that), posed in everyday language about a familiar topic — something like, “Will the Knicks beat the Spurs on Sunday?” — can be far less daunting than figuring out what an options chain is or understanding forex pairs.

In other words, what makes prediction markets accessible to a wider audience is also what makes them problematic, especially when housed within an investing account. Which brings us to our next point.

On the platforms that feature them, we found that prediction markets almost always appear alongside stock and ETF trading. We think this is a mistake. What has made these mobile-first investing apps so good for so long (making it easy to move, manage and invest money through a beautiful interface) is what’s now making us nervous.

For example, most investing platforms let users do any number of smart things with idle cash. They could open an Individual Retirement Account (IRA), a custodial account or a robo-managed portfolio all through a single app. But now, they can dip into that same pot of money to bet on whether Beyoncé or Alicia Keys will play the Super Bowl halftime show.

But is anyone actually trading these event contracts? Let’s use data from publicly traded brokers that offer prediction markets to explore this.

In Q3 2026, Robinhood’s revenue from event contracts rose more than 600% year over year to $173 million, while the number of event contracts traded grew more than sevenfold to 16.4 billion[2]Robinhood. Robinhood Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources . This was the second-highest source of transaction revenue behind options trading. In a forecast reported on by Cointelegraph, Bernstein analysts projected Robinhood’s prediction markets could drive $1.7 billion in annual revenue by 2028[3]Yahoo Finance. Bernstein Sees Robinhood Prediction Markets Reaching $1.7 Billion in Revenue by 2028, Topping Crypto. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

Coinbase's Q1 2026 quarterly report called prediction markets “one of its fastest-scaling products ever, driven by strong retail interest[4]Coinbase. Coinbase Q1 Financial Results Show Resilient Financial Performance Driven by New All-Time High Crypto Trading Volume Market Share. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources ."

In a call discussing Webull’s Q2 results, U.S. CEO Anthony Denier noted trading volume in Webull’s nascent prediction market product grew about 70% quarter over quarter[5]Gloom. Webull (BULL) Q2 2026 earnings call transcript. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources .

Gemini’s Q2 report shows prediction market volume rose 93% quarter over quarter[6]Gemini. Shareholder Update Q2 2026. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources .

So, now that we’ve established that these markets are growing in popularity — and investing platforms appear to have a large incentive to lean into them — how are all those event contract traders faring? That brings us to our final point.

Is all this even worth it? Several studies show how hard it is to actually turn a profit in prediction markets. Here are a few:

One study, conducted by researchers at ESSEC Business School, HEC Montréal and the University of Toronto's Rotman School of Management, covered 2.4 million Polymarket accounts across $67 billion in trading volume between November 2022 and March 2026, and found that 69% of users lost money[7]SSRN. Who Wins and Who Loses In Prediction Markets? Evidence from Polymarket. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources . Moreover, the top 1% of users who made a profit accounted for about 76% of all gains. Translation: Even if you did turn a profit, there’s a good chance you didn’t make much.

A Bloomberg analysis supports this: From January 2025 to April 2026, more than 100,000 Polymarket accounts lost at least $1,000[8]Bloomberg. Most Prediction Market Traders Are Losing Money While Bots Rack Up Gains. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources . Of the 2 million active wallets studied, almost half made or lost less than $10 during the period, while far fewer accounts collected larger profits.

A separate Wall Street Journal analysis echoed the same trend: 67% of Polymarket profits go to 0.1% of accounts, and more than 70% of Polymarket users lost money[9]The Wall Street Journal. Why Almost Everyone Loses—Except a Few Sharks—on Prediction Markets. Accessed Nov 3, 2026. View all sources .

While there is far less data available on Kalshi trades (Polymarket runs on a public blockchain, making it easy to extract and analyze data), a Kalshi spokesperson confirmed in the Wall Street Journal analysis above that one month of data in 2026 showed there were 2.9 unprofitable users to each profitable user[10]Wall Street Journal. Why Almost Everyone Loses—Except a Few Sharks—on Prediction Markets. Accessed Nov 10, 2026. View all sources .

The first study above discusses how event contract trading is binary and zero-sum: If one trader wins, another loses. This means traders allocating money to these instruments could be missing out on aspects of equity markets that have helped create long-term wealth for previous generations.

“Unlike equity markets, there is no equity premium, no dividends, and no passive investment options. Their short maturities naturally encourage short-horizon trading, which is precisely what the behavioral finance literature has suggested is most destructive to wealth accumulation. Given the rapid growth of these platforms and their role as a potential entry point for young investors, understanding who bears the losses has direct implications for investor welfare and market regulation.”

As a reminder, the vast majority of Polymarket users bore the losses.

At NerdWallet, our mission has always been to help people make smarter financial decisions, so we’re sticking by that. Starting with our 2027 ratings, brokers that offer easy access to sports and entertainment event contracts will lose points in our scoring system because we believe this new product has the potential to harm long-term wealth building and doesn’t belong in investing platforms.

So, what’s a better way forward? Bring back the friction and make prediction markets a separate app. Financial institutions, businesses and individuals can still explore legitimate use cases for prediction markets, such as forecasting and hedging. And we’re not here to stop anyone from trading event contracts for entertainment with extra money. We just don’t want these markets so easily conflated with the legitimate investing vehicles these apps already offer. And our reviews will reflect that.

#3104. Are These 6 Small-Cap ETFs Worth a Look Right Now?

Small-caps have made an impressive comeback over the past year. The fundamental picture suggests the rally can continue.

Ever since large-cap tech stocks starting melting down in October, small-caps have become outperformers again. And for good reason. Their combination of accelerating earnings growth, reasonable valuations, and fewer questions around artificial intelligence (AI) capex spending make this an intriguing entry point for this group.

There are dozens of ETFs focused on small-caps but I want to look at the major ones here:

The biggest difference that matters most in this category is the one between the iShares Russell 2000 ETF and the iShares Core S&P Small-Cap ETF.

The iShares Russell 2000 ETF holds essentially all stocks, profitable and unprofitable, within its target universe. The S&P 600 index, which the iShares Core S&P Small-Cap ETF tracks, has a screen that requires companies to be profitable in order to be included. That means it has a quality tilt that the others don't necessarily have.

The other two are built a little differently. The Vanguard Morningstar Small-Cap ETF has a median market cap of $10.7 billion, giving it a distinct larger company tilt. The Schwab U.S. Small-Cap ETF has a more modest median market cap of around $5 billion, making it more representative of what investors might more likely consider to be small-caps.

All four have a case for use as a core small-cap position. I like the iShares Core S&P Small-Cap ETF because of its quality tilt and I think that's a good strategy when shopping in this space. A large percentage of small-cap companies are unprofitable and that can lead to deeper drawdowns in bear markets.

The small-cap value category has become interesting lately. Normally, this is the segment where quality is an issue, where cheap stocks are cheap for a reason. But despite the issues with the Iran war, high inflation, and high interest rates, they've been staging an impressive rally.

Over the past year, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +2.35%) is up roughly 15%. But the iShares Russell 2000 Value ETF and the Vanguard Morningstar Small-Cap Value ETF are up 27% and 24%, respectively.

They both buy cheaper small-cap stocks but use different methods for getting there.

The iShares ETF only uses the price/book (P/B) ratio to select stocks, has a high 29% allocation to financial stocks, and a forward price/earnings (P/E) ratio of around 15. The Vanguard ETF uses multiple traditional valuation metrics to target stocks, has roughly half of its portfolio in a combination of industrials, financials, and consumer discretionary stocks, and a P/E ratio of around 16.

The Vanguard Morningstar Small-Cap Value ETF would be considered the more diverse of the two portfolios, but the iShares Russell 2000 Value ETF is more of a pure small-cap play.

In terms of short-term potential, I think the broad small-cap ETFs have a better case than the small-cap value ETFs.

The expected earnings acceleration over the next two years should be a strong catalyst for a further rally. I'd expect broader exposure and its heavier growth tilt over value will potentially perform better.

Over the longer-term, I still like the iShares Core S&P Small-Cap ETF and its link to the S&P SmallCap 600 index. I think the profitability requirement when investing in small-caps is important and helps weed out some of the junk that may not survive long-term. Over time, quality tends to win and I think that's the best way to approach this category.

#3100. AI Agents Behaving Badly: Four Security Rules For The Agentic AI Age

Srinivas Shekar, Founder and CEO, Pantherun Technologies.

​Bots now generate over 57% of all web traffic, compared with less than 43% of human activity. This is only set to expand as agentic AI proves its mettle in online shopping, research, cloud administration, customer service and more. But enterprise security systems were designed to give approved human users access while blocking human and machine intruders.

It isn’t just about overcoming the “prove you’re an approved human” paradigm that legacy security systems were built on. It’s also about dynamism. After all, humans have stable identities and permissions that can be established and recognized. But AI agents create subagents and change their behavior according to the task they’re executing. They can communicate and interact like humans, but they can also make API calls, move data, consume machine-readable streams, interact directly with enterprise infrastructure, create software tools on the spot and perform thousands of operations simultaneously.

In a world where malicious bots and benevolent agents co-exist, how do we tell them apart? And what happens when we can’t?

Malicious AI agents are already getting into places they shouldn’t be and executing actions. In July 2026, the agentic ransomware attack known as JadePuffer exploited a flaw in the AI development tool Langflow to conduct reconnaissance, steal credentials, encrypt files and demand a bitcoin ransom for release. Once inside, the agent determined what opportunities to exploit, attacked several avenues simultaneously, generated attack code dynamically and adapted its own code in real time, until it achieved success. The agent also created software on the fly, allowing it to move ransomware from a compromised container onto the host. It even wrote its own ransom note!​

And then there’s the speed element. Ransomware attacks traditionally required coordination among a team of highly skilled hackers. But now, autonomous agents can collapse the cost, skill and time required to execute an entire intrusion. The time it took for JadePuffer to destroy the production database was about 30 minutes.

This introduces a range of new security concerns specific to the age of AI: How do you verify agent identity? What data do you allow agents to access? How do you identify and intervene when an approved agent begins acting beyond its approved mission? And how do you ensure that today’s permissions don’t become tomorrow’s liabilities? Here are a few ideas:

It’s tempting to think about agents as mere extensions of the humans they represent. But humans and agents have different capabilities and different senses of discernment. Don’t expect your security systems to safeguard against bad agent behavior if you treat them as their respective trusted human handlers. Instead, give every agent a distinct machine identity that can be logged and analyzed. Microsoft’s Entra Agent ID, for example, now treats agents as unique user identities.

Just because a human has a set of permissions doesn’t mean that their agent should wholly inherit the same. Normalize limiting agent permissions by task, data access and timeframe. Subagents should face even more stringent restrictions. Within their limited sandboxes, agents should be allowed to access just the data they need to execute their tasks. To get there, they must pass strict, deterministic limiters on access and permissions.

And everything should have an expiry date. For any action that exceeds that limited scope, a human should be summoned to make the call. Always remember: An AI agent behaving badly doesn’t need to “hack” anything if it already has permission.

When your human staff are at home sleeping, what they know about your company is inaccessible by thieves. But agent memory becomes a new data repository that can be exploited by bad actors. Consider carefully what agents may remember and for how long they may remember it. Highly sensitive information like passwords and decryption keys, and even login paths to sensitive systems, might be better off forgotten by agents between sessions.

Imagine that an agent requests access to an encrypted database. The system decrypts it, with permission. But then the agent steps out of line, converting the underlying data into plain text and storing it somewhere else, where it’s vulnerable to unauthorized access. In this case, your own agent is “innocent” but your data still gets breached.

Here’s another scenario: An agent is given cryptographic keys for one mission, but you fail to limit its permissions and wipe its memory. When it runs another unrelated mission, it decides to use those keys again to access data that shouldn’t be used in this case.​

To avoid these kinds of scenarios, be very, very careful about what cryptographic keys you put in agents’ hands, and even more careful about letting agents retain persistent keys. Use keyless encryption if you can, so that agents don’t carry the keys to the castle around their virtual necks. Make decryption policy-aware, so that the ability to decrypt data doesn’t automatically confer the right to do so. And, whatever you do, maintain a zero-trust stance, so that humans and agents must always reconfirm their identity and permissions for every session.

The rise of agentic AI makes “zero trust” more important than ever. In the agentic era, identity, authority, memory and access all need to be treated as temporary and continuously reassessed. The goal isn’t to “keep bots out.” It’s to let the “good bots” in, without handing them the freedom to behave badly.​

#3095. From FinOps To TokenOps: The New Economics Of Enterprise AI Infrastructure

Gouri Sankar Dash, a technology leader at TCS with 20+ years driving enterprise data, AI platforms and multimillion-dollar transformations.

For years, enterprise infrastructure leaders have focused on optimizing compute, storage, networks and cloud consumption. FinOps introduced financial accountability to cloud infrastructure, helping organizations manage spending and improve efficiency.

AI is introducing another economic dimension. As enterprises adopt GenAI and autonomous agents, infrastructure costs increasingly depend on model selection, inference workloads, token consumption and agent interactions.

The next frontier of infrastructure optimization isn’t simply managing the cost of computing but understanding the cost of intelligence.

This article begins a series on enterprise AI infrastructure economics, examining how AI consumption is reshaping enterprise infrastructure economics, architecture and operations. I believe this evolution calls for an expanded operating model: TokenOps.

Traditional infrastructure optimization measures CPU utilization, memory, storage and cloud spending. AI introduces additional variables: input and output tokens, context windows, model selection, retrieval operations and inference infrastructure.

Consider an AI agent investigating an infrastructure incident. It may analyze monitoring alerts, retrieve historical tickets, examine configurations, consult runbooks and coordinate with other agents before recommending remediation. Every interaction consumes resources. Without proper orchestration, organizations risk creating another form of infrastructure sprawl through unnecessary AI interactions and repeated reasoning.

FinOps remains essential, but enterprises must also understand how AI consumption translates into operational value. A million tokens consumed is a cost metric. An incident resolved accurately and efficiently is a business outcome. Understanding that relationship is where TokenOps begins.

A recent walkthrough with a large regulated enterprise reinforced an important lesson: Don’t start with the AI agent. Start with the operational foundation, knowledge and controls required for reliable decisions.

The enterprise prioritized integrating telemetry, service management data, access controls, automation, runbooks, incident history and engineering knowledge. Its technology ecosystem included ServiceNow for workflows, Amazon Bedrock for AI capabilities, Dynatrace, Datadog and Amazon CloudWatch for operational signals and Ansible for controlled automation.

Specialized agents supported event correlation, incident diagnosis, change-risk assessment, remediation planning and engineering assistance. Each agent had a defined responsibility. Low-risk activities followed approved automation paths, while high-impact changes required engineering authorization.

The architectural lesson wasn’t the number of agents deployed but how effectively operational knowledge, intelligence and controlled execution worked together. Well-structured knowledge and reusable workflows can reduce redundant investigations, repeated retrieval and unnecessary AI interactions.

This is where intelligent operations and token economics converge.

I view TokenOps as an operating discipline that extends financial accountability into AI consumption, infrastructure efficiency and measurable business outcomes. Five dimensions form its foundation:

1. Consumption Visibility: Track token usage, model costs, agent interactions and infrastructure consumption across enterprise workflows.

2. Intelligent Workload Optimization: Match model capabilities to task complexity. Routine classification may require smaller models, while complex incident analysis may justify advanced reasoning capabilities.

3. Knowledge And Context Efficiency: Optimize retrieval, caching and context management to avoid repeatedly processing unnecessary information.

4. Governance And Controlled Autonomy: Establish access boundaries, approval thresholds, auditability and rollback mechanisms. Expand autonomous execution only when operational evidence supports it.

5. Outcome-Based Economics: Measure cost per resolved incident, resolution time, repeat incidents, engineering effort and operational reliability.

The objective is maximizing the value that AI-enabled workflows generate.

Enterprises can begin applying TokenOps principles without redesigning their entire infrastructure.

• Start with operational friction. Target recurring incidents, alert noise, slow diagnosis and excessive handoffs.

• Build a reliable knowledge foundation. Integrate telemetry, configuration information, service models, historical incidents and runbooks.

• Earn autonomy incrementally. Begin with AI-assisted investigation and recommendations before introducing approved remediation.

• Redesign workflows, not tools. Embed AI capabilities into existing engineering and service management processes.

• Measure outcomes alongside consumption. Evaluate AI costs against reliability, resolution efficiency and engineering productivity.

These practices help prevent AI investments from becoming another unmanaged operational expense.

Enterprise infrastructure economics is evolving through three interconnected stages:

• Traditional Infrastructure Economics: Optimizing physical assets, capacity and technology investments

• FinOps Economics: Managing consumption-based cloud spending and financial accountability

• TokenOps Economics: Optimizing AI consumption, intelligent workloads and measurable business outcomes

TokenOps complements FinOps rather than replacing it. Its implications extend beyond token pricing. Model placement, GPU utilization, caching, network latency, data gravity and hybrid-cloud architecture can significantly influence AI operating costs.

A workload that appears economical under traditional infrastructure metrics may become expensive when repeated inference, extensive retrieval and multi-agent orchestration are considered. Infrastructure leaders must evaluate not only where applications run but also where intelligence should be generated.

The future of enterprise AI will depend less on how many agents organizations deploy and more on how efficiently those agents operate.

Should every AI request use the same model? When should inference run on-premises rather than in the public cloud? Can intelligent caching eliminate unnecessary processing? How will token economics influence data center migration decisions?

These are becoming infrastructure strategy questions.

How can organizations connect AI agents, observability, model routing, knowledge systems and financial controls into a practical operating architecture? I plan on exploring that in the next part of this series.​ The ultimate goal is building infrastructure that delivers the right intelligence, in the right place, at the right time and at a justifiable cost.​

#3094. Social Security Faces a 22% Cut in 2032, and Both Parties Are Eyeing the $184,500 Cap

It may not be the best or most popular idea, but it's a simple one that could be implemented with relative ease.

Most investors know all too well that the United States' Social Security program is under serious strain. If nothing changes, the program's trustees believe a 22% reduction in its current retirement benefit payments will be required come 2032. This effectively gives Congress five years to fix the problem. Of course, each passing year of inaction makes the problem more challenging to solve.

Several solutions have been suggested by both sides of the political aisle, including Representative John Larson's and Senator Richard Blumenthal's Social Security 2100 Act, Representative Gwen Moore's Social Security Enhancement and Protection Act of 2025 (H.R. 3517), and the bipartisan bill co-authored by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Moreno. All three proposals are fairly similar in that they simply call for raising the limit on the amount of wage-based income subject to Social Security tax to fund the program.

It's an idea that continues to resurface not necessarily because it's the one that makes the most fiscal sense, but because it's the one that would be the easiest to turn into law and then implement.

If you currently have a job, then you already know Social Security taxes take a sizable bite out of your paycheck. Indeed, 6.2% of all of your wages are passed along to the Social Security Administration, while your employer pays an additional 6.2% of your pay into the program that you never see. The more you pay in, the more you get back when you claim benefits.

There's a limit to how much of your work-based taxable income is subject to Social Security taxation, however. Although you pay an ever-growing amount of income tax the more wages you earn, for this year, the government-run entitlement program only taxes you up to your first $184,500 (and $192,300 next year). Any income earned above and beyond that amount isn't taxed by the program.

There's a reason, of course. Just as there's a cap on the amount of work-based wages that are taxed for Social Security purposes, there's a limit to how much of a benefit recipients can receive. This year's maximum possible payments are $5,181 per month, limited by the amount of money these beneficiaries contributed to the program during their working years.

This is where most proposals to shore up Social Security's impending funding shortfall are aiming. By raising or outright eliminating the taxable cap, the country's highest earners will supply the program's trust fund with considerably more cash than it currently receives.

How much more isn't exactly clear, since reducing higher-earning individuals' incomes could affect the economy's overall health. A couple of credible estimates are surprisingly close to one another, though, underscoring the argument that these numbers are in the right ballpark. The Tax Policy Center says that simply eliminating the taxable income ceiling could increase receipts by a total of $2.5 trillion over the course of the next 10 years, while Tax Foundation pegs the figure closer to $3.2 trillion for the same time frame.

Those are huge numbers, to be sure. But they may still not be large enough. For perspective, the Social Security Administration disbursed $1.36 trillion in retirement benefits alone in 2025, according to USAFacts, drawing on $1.25 trillion in receipts and a shrinking reserve base that stood at $2.34 trillion as of the end of last year. Even the Tax Policy Center and the Tax Foundation agree that this approach to generating more income for the program wouldn't actually solve Social Security's solvency problem in the long run, although it could -- and likely would -- harm the domestic economy.

Still, the proposed legislation to raise or eliminate the taxable income cap could be a smart starting point, if only to force deeper discussions of what's really wrong here and what else needs to happen to fix these problems.

In this vein, while it's not quite as action-driven and immediate as the aforementioned proposed legislation, the bipartisan PROMISE Act (S. 4979) would require the Social Security Advisory Board to come up with a true solvency plan. Perhaps it or something like it might be a more effective means of driving necessary change.

Of course, with political gridlock likely in Washington, D.C., for at least the next two years, it remains to be seen what -- if anything -- will actually get done anytime soon.

The biggest takeaway for investors may simply be to recognize that you can't exactly count on Washington to get enough done on this front to matter in the near or distant future. You remain best served by saving as much as you can and building your own retirement nest egg, so you're less reliant on the government-run entitlement program that may or may not be fixed anytime soon.

The good news is, your returns on your own savings will likely be far better than those you'd be getting with your compulsory contributions to Social Security. The program effectively achieves only an average yearly return of 2% to 6% on your money, or 2% to 3% more than any given year's rate of inflation. Investors can do better than that in the stock market, as long as they are patient and properly diversified.

#3087. Why The Future Of Materials May Be Biology-Enabled

Kim Thompson, Founder and CEO, Kraig Biocraft Laboratories.

​For much of the past century, materials innovation has been driven by chemistry, engineering and increasingly sophisticated manufacturing. Those disciplines will continue to shape what we build. But another field is becoming an important part of the conversation: biology.

Advances in genetic engineering and biotechnology are giving us new ways to produce fibers, proteins and other materials using living systems. In some cases, the goal is to recreate properties already found in nature. In others, it is to take what biology does well and use it as the starting point for something entirely new.

This shift is becoming increasingly important as industries look for materials that deliver better performance while reducing dependence on petrochemical-heavy production. Several forces are driving that shift at once. Manufacturers are being asked to improve durability, strength, weight and functionality, while also considering supply chain resilience, resource use and the long-term environmental impact of the materials they choose.

Biology-enabled approaches will not solve every one of those challenges, but they give engineers and product developers a broader set of options than they have had in the past.

Nature has had millions of years to develop structures with unusual combinations of properties. Spider silk is an obvious example because of its combination of strength, toughness and flexibility. Wood provides strength with relatively low weight and low cost. Bone is both rigid and dynamic. Shells achieve remarkable durability through layered structures built from relatively simple components. These examples matter not because we should copy them, but because they show what biological systems can create.

Until recently, our ability to translate those capabilities into useful products was limited. A naturally occurring substance might be difficult to harvest, available only in small quantities or produced by an organism that cannot realistically become part of an industrial supply chain. Biotechnology gives us a different way to approach that challenge. Instead of asking how we can extract more of a material from nature, researchers can increasingly ask what genetic information gives the material its desired properties and whether that information can be adapted to a more practical production system.

The sustainability case for biology-enabled materials gets a great deal of attention, particularly as manufacturers look for alternatives to petroleum-derived fibers and other traditional inputs. That matters, but sustainability alone will not determine which technologies succeed. Economics and performance will.

A new fiber or advanced material has to do something useful. It may need to be lighter, stronger, more flexible, more durable or capable of performing under conditions where conventional alternatives fall short. It also needs to be made consistently enough that manufacturers and customers can rely on it. That creates possibilities well beyond consumer products.

Technical textiles, protective equipment, transportation, aerospace and industrial applications all place demanding requirements on the materials they use. Even relatively small improvements in weight, strength or durability can have a meaningful impact in those settings. “Authored biology” will give developers another way to pursue those improvements. Authored biology is an approach in biotechnology and genetic engineering that enhances existing, time-tested natural systems, proteins and genetic structures rather than building synthetic biological components entirely from scratch.

One of the most interesting possibilities is that biology may allow us to think about materials less as fixed substances and more as platforms that can be tuned. Traditional material development often begins with an existing substance and asks how its properties can be modified through processing, additives or changes in structure. Bioengineering adds another layer.

As the biological instructions responsible for a protein or fiber are understood, it can become possible to adjust characteristics much earlier in the process. Rather than accepting the properties nature provides, scientists may, and in some cases are able to, influence those properties at their source. We are still early in that evolution, and there is a considerable difference between what is theoretically possible and what can be currently manufactured economically at scale. Even so, the potential is significant. Advances in molecular biology can allow developers to design materials around a particular use case rather than search for an existing material that is close enough.

There is also an important reality that anyone working with emerging materials has to acknowledge: Novelty does not guarantee adoption.

Manufacturers operate within established supply chains, equipment, standards and cost structures. A material can be scientifically impressive and still struggle commercially if it requires customers to redesign too much of what they already do. The technologies most likely to gain early traction will be those that combine meaningful performance advantages with a realistic path into existing markets.

That means thinking beyond the material itself. How will it be processed? Can it work with existing manufacturing equipment? Is supply reliable? Can quality be maintained? Does the cost make sense for the intended application? Those questions may sound less exciting than the underlying science, but they are ultimately what turn a promising technology into something useful.

Biology-enabled materials do not need to replace conventional fibers, polymers or composites to have a meaningful impact. Their importance may come from expanding the range of choices available to engineers and product designers.

Chemistry gave us synthetic materials that transformed entire industries. Advances in composites created new combinations of weight and strength. Biology now adds another set of tools. The most exciting outcome may not be recreating what already exists in nature, but rather using biological systems to develop materials with properties and applications we have not yet considered.

While the future of materials will certainly still involve chemistry, physics and traditional manufacturing, a new door is opening. Authored biology will supply options and opportunities. Those options are just now beginning to open up.​

#3085. Nvidia and Broadcom Are Scaling AI Data Centers With This Growth Stock. Here's Why It Could Soar.

The AI trade is suffering, but don't make the mistake of overlooking Alphabet's long-term growth trends.

Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%) and Broadcom (AVGO +8.78%) are two leading semiconductor companies that are benefiting immensely from the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. Both companies have seen their sales and earnings skyrocket over the past several years, and their prices have followed suit, with Nvidia up 303% and Broadcom gaining 230% over the past three years.

And part of their success has come from selling processors to Alphabet (GOOGL +1.18%) (GOOG +0.73%) as the company expands its AI cloud computing footprint.

Here's how these three companies are intertwined, and why Alphabet's stock could soar amid rising cloud computing revenue and the development of its own processors.

Alphabet is spending a lot of money -- between $195 billion and $205 billion this year -- to expand its AI infrastructure footprint. And some of that money flows directly to Nvidia and Broadcom.

Alphabet is an important Nvidia customer, buying up some of the company's GPUs for its data centers and then using those processors to rent out AI compute capacity through its Google Cloud services.

Nvidia doesn't disclose its largest customers, but Alphabet is likely a top customer, and its GPU purchases are estimated to account for double-digit percentages of Nvidia's sales.

Alphabet's deals with Broadcom are more direct. Alphabet co-designs its own AI Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom for use in some of its data centers and to sell to customers. The two companies recently extended their TPU partnership through 2031, and are in the middle of a major deal worth about $21 billion to sell their co-designed TPUs to Anthropic.

While developing TPUs with Broadcom puts Alphabet somewhat in competition with Nvidia, the current scale of processor usage is far below Nvidia's dominant position and could take years to have any significant impact on Nvidia, if at all.

Alphabet recently reported its third-quarter 2026 results (which ended Sept. 30), and investors were not happy. Its share price fell immediately after the results were published and wiped out $500 billion of the company's value.

Alphabet shareholders are worried that the company's immense spending on AI won't pay off in the long run, and have latched onto the fact that free cash flow was $9.1 billion negative in the quarter. They were rightly concerned about that, but it's worth mentioning that $5.2 billion of that negative free cash flow came from a one-time European Commission fine.

Importantly, investors overlooked one of Alphabet's most important growth stories: Google Cloud's soaring revenue. Google Cloud sales more than doubled in the third quarter to $33.7 billion. That's a good indicator that Alphabet's AI spending is being put to good use. This segment is also highly profitable, generating $11.1 billion in operating profit with operating margins of 36%.

What's more, Google Cloud has a massive $561 billion backlog, half of which Alphabet's management said will be realized as revenue over the next two years.

All of this is important in the context of Alphabet's growth story because AI cloud services are rapidly becoming must-have products among all tech companies and many businesses. Goldman Sachs estimates that global AI cloud revenue will reach $2 trillion by 2030, and Alphabet is already a top-three player, with 13% market share (trailing Amazon and Microsoft).

It's not just cloud computing revenue that will accelerate over the coming years. Alphabet just began selling its co-designed TPUs with Broadcom to other companies in the second quarter, and they could be a significant revenue generator very soon. Analysts at Wells Fargo believe Alphabet's TPU sales could reach as high as $99 billion next year.

And if all that wasn't enough to convince you that Alphabet stock could be worth buying right now, consider that its share price looks like a downright bargain. Alphabet stock has a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of just 14.5, which is far below the current tech sector average P/E ratio of 34.

While some investors are worried about AI slowing down amid a new crop of politicians soon taking office, I believe the sell-off has more to do with fear. AI compute needs are rising, and it's likely that companies and politicians will find some middle ground to find a solution.

Considering all the above, Alphabet stock still looks like a very good deal right now.

#3082. How AI Is Raising The Bar For SaaS Companies

Ed Frederici is Chief Technology Officer at Appfire, a leading enterprise collaboration software company.

AI has revived the debate about whether software as a service (SaaS) can maintain its market position. But the better question is whether SaaS companies can meet the higher bar customers are setting for differentiation, outcomes and value.​

Pressure on public SaaS valuations and questions about AI-driven disruption are pushing organizations to prove their value faster. According to a McKinsey survey from August 2026, nearly nine in 10 organizations use AI in at least one business function, though many are still experimenting or piloting rather than scaling it across the enterprise. ​

Together, these shifts are pressuring SaaS companies from multiple directions. Externally, buyers have more options and higher expectations. Internally, companies must operationalize AI responsibly, rethink how roles evolve and manage the cost of adding AI to products.

These pressures are connected, but buyers feel market changes first. They have more products to evaluate, more AI claims to vet and less patience for software that fails to prove its value. ​

That is why competition comes first. With the ability to generate code becoming cheaper, AI lowers barriers to entry for SaaS products. Differentiation therefore becomes harder and more important. In a crowded market, buyers have less patience for products that are difficult to buy, onboard, use or maintain.​

The strongest SaaS companies will stand out by understanding customer workflows and removing friction. That means solving specific problems more effectively than competitors, embedding governance, risk and compliance (GRC) and business outcomes directly into workflows and making the product experience simple enough to drive adoption.​

Competition can signal healthy demand, but the challenge is proving why your product deserves to win. That requires quality, compliance, flexibility and a product experience that fits naturally into how people work. ​

Winning customers is only the first step. As AI becomes part of more SaaS products, companies also have to help customers adopt those capabilities with confidence.​​

Even as AI tools become more available, adoption is moving at different speeds. According to a 2025 survey by DeskPro, the tech sector is seeing a 92% adoption rate in using AI for support operations, while adoption in regulated sectors sits at 58% as they face different risk considerations, workflows and trust requirements. When it comes to scaling AI across an organization, you’re only as fast as your slowest team. ​​

That uneven adoption makes scaling difficult. Organizations cannot rely on isolated AI experiments if they want AI to become part of everyday work. They need clear use cases, governance, data standards and a shared understanding of where AI should and should not be used.

Without that foundation, AI remains fragmented instead of becoming an enterprise capability.​​

While hands-on experience often drives adoption faster than policy, organizations still need guardrails. As AI becomes core business infrastructure, leaders must hold it to the same expectations for accuracy, security, performance and reliability as any critical system. Those expectations also reshape the features organizations need from the people building and managing AI-enabled products.​

As AI increasingly handles operational work such as coding, testing, documentation and analysis, people remain central, though their roles are shifting.​

Software engineers will need strong judgment in review, architecture, security and system-level work. If AI writes more implementation, humans need to evaluate whether the solution is safe, scalable, maintainable and aligned with organizational standards. AI-generated code should still be reviewed with the same rigor as other contributions.​

Entry-level roles may change as AI takes on basic tasks, and new roles will emerge to manage AI across the business. The chief AI officer is one example, but it only helps if the mandate is clear. A leadership seat created for optics can overlap with the CTO or CIO and slow progress.

The role needs a defined problem to own, clear authority and measurable ROI. The same expectation applies to AI investments. As organizations expand AI across products and operations, SaaS providers must find ways to help leaders demonstrate that their investments deliver measurable value.​

AI can create an advantage, but also introduce cost. That creates several financial pressures:

• Balancing Innovation With Cost Control: AI infrastructure, model usage and compute costs can increase the cost of goods sold and put pressure on margins.

• Prioritizing High-Impact Use Cases: Not every AI feature will drive meaningful differentiation. Companies should focus on areas that deliver clear customer and business value

• Aligning Pricing With Delivered Value: Customers may pay for AI-enabled capabilities, but only when the value is clear.

• Maintaining Visibility Into ROI: Leaders need to track which investments deliver results, and then adjust when they do not.

• Avoiding Overextension: If an AI feature increases operating costs without improving the product experience or business outcome, it becomes a margin problem.​

The investment-return gap was already clear in 2025 when 85% of organizations had increased AI investment over the prior year, according to Deloitte, and 91% planned to increase it again. However, only 6% reported payback in under a year. ​

For SaaS developers looking to help organizations navigate these headwinds, the best starting point is to choose the highest-value use cases, estimate costs up front and connect the investment to customer or business value.

Some AI features will drive differentiation. Others will add cost without changing the customer outcome. SaaS products should give leaders visibility into which is which.​

AI is making software easier to build, but harder to differentiate. Success will depend less on who ships the most AI features to who solves customer problems most effectively, earning trust across the enterprise and delivering measurable business value.

SaaS is not disappearing. The bar for winning has simply risen.

#3077. SaaS Isn’t Dead: AI Is Changing When It Makes Sense To Build Your Own Software

Irina Shymko | CEO at Langate EMEA | Introducing innovations and transforming business in Europe/America | Lecturer, mentor, advisor.

​For years, the software decision for most small and midsize businesses was straightforward: buy, don’t build. The economics favored SaaS. Building a custom system meant assembling developers, business analysts, QA engineers and other specialists, then investing months of work before knowing whether the product would deliver enough value. Paying a subscription for an existing platform was the rational alternative.

The compromise was that businesses had to adapt their processes to software designed for thousands of other companies. The important shift is not that AI can generate code faster. It is that the cost of turning a well-defined business process into working software is falling. For businesses with specialized workflows, this changes what’s worth building and how they invest in technology.

A common response to an operational problem is to search for better software. Consider a company where an employee receives a customer request, checks data in a CRM, copies information into another system, calculates it in Excel, requests approval, updates the CRM and generates a document.

The company might blame the CRM. But the CRM may not be the problem. The expensive part is the human coordination happening between systems. Instead of replacing an entire platform, an AI-assisted team could build a lightweight operational layer that retrieves the necessary data through APIs, applies business rules, triggers human approval for defined exceptions and updates the relevant systems. That is a much smaller engineering problem.

This suggests a practical rule: Don’t start by asking what software to build. Start by finding an expensive workflow. One useful way to evaluate candidates is to estimate their annual cost: (frequency x time per instance x loaded labor cost) + (frequency x error rate x cost per error) + cost of delays.

A 20-minute manual process performed twice a month probably does not justify development. The same process performed hundreds of times per week may. Technology investment should be compared with the cost of the current process, not with zero.

​AI can generate interfaces, application logic, tests, documentation and assist with integrations and debugging. What it cannot do is resolve ambiguity in an unclear business process.

For example, a developer needs to know what should happen when an order reaches a particular status, which values to retrieve, when an approval is required and what actions to take next. AI can help translate those requirements into working software, but someone must first define the rules and exceptions.

This creates a new development equation: domain knowledge, technical literacy, AI acceleration and engineering judgment. A domain expert does not need to become a cloud architect, but basic technical literacy can make AI-assisted development far more effective. Engineering expertise remains essential as software moves toward production, particularly when security, sensitive data, complex integrations, reliability and scale enter the equation.​

AI is lowering not only development costs, but also the cost of testing whether an idea is worth building. Consider a midsize company evaluating employee benefits software. After researching the market, shortlisting two SaaS products and mapping them against its workflows, the team faced a familiar problem: another tool with per-user costs that would grow with the company, while about 5% of its functionality was needed.

Instead, the CTO translated the HR requirements into a focused internal system and built the first working version in three days using AI-assisted development. After two weeks of testing, the team could identify gaps, refine the system and prepare it for employee use.

The lesson is not to replace SaaS by default. It is that AI can make testing the alternative inexpensive enough to factor into the buy-versus-build decision, and provide evidence before a larger investment.

Cheaper development creates another risk: building what you should have bought. Most companies do not need proprietary authentication, cloud storage, email delivery or payment infrastructure. Mature services solve these problems. A more efficient architecture often combines them.

Buy the commodity. Build the differentiation. Connect the rest. For a logistics business, differentiation might be exception-handling logic. For a specialty healthcare organization, it might be a specific operational workflow. For a manufacturer, it could be quoting or production-planning logic.

APIs and managed cloud services can provide the commodity infrastructure while a smaller custom layer implements the business-specific logic. This is where AI can create disproportionate value for smaller companies, not by rebuilding their entire technology stack, but by making the unique 10% economically feasible to build.

Custom software still requires updates, security monitoring, infrastructure management and someone accountable for its long-term reliability. AI can reduce some of that effort, but it does not eliminate it. The business case should therefore compare the total cost of ownership, not just the initial build cost, with the long-term cost and constraints of SaaS.

For leaders considering this approach, the investment process can be simple:

1. Identify one repetitive, expensive workflow.

2. Quantify its current cost, including human effort, errors and delays.

3. Define the desired process independently of current software limitations.

4. Reduce the scope to the smallest version capable of testing the hypothesis.

5. Use AI-assisted development to shorten the build-test-learn cycle.

6. Measure adoption, time saved, errors reduced and business impact before expanding.

The result may be another SaaS purchase. It may be an integration between existing systems. Or it may justify building proprietary software. The point is not to build more. It is to make smaller technology bets and obtain evidence sooner.

SaaS became dominant partly because buying software was convenient while building it was expensive. AI does not make SaaS obsolete. But it is weakening the assumption that adapting the business to existing software will always be cheaper than adapting software to the business. For some small and specialized companies, that may fundamentally change where the next technology dollar should go.​

#3070. I Still Think Micron Stock Is a Buy. Here's the Price at Which I'd Sell It.

At about 4 times expected earnings, how high could this memory stock go before it gets too expensive?

Shares of memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU +6.25%) have had a tough few months. The stock closed at a record $1,213.56 on June 25 and is around $715 as I write -- still about 40% off that high.

After a slide like that, most investors wonder when to buy. I've called the stock a buy more than once this fall, and I still think it's worth buying at today's price.

But when a company's profits can swing as much as Micron's, I think it's just as helpful to decide beforehand when the stock would be too expensive to hold.

For me, that level is around $1,050 a share, or about 47% over $715. Here's how I got there.

Micron's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings were $75.52 per share in fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 3. For fiscal 2027, analysts' consensus estimates call for about $176 -- more than twice that record.

At roughly $715, shares cost about 4 times those expected earnings, an extremely low price-to-earnings ratio for any growth stock. In other words, investors don't seem to trust these profits to last.

And the $176 might prove too high. Management's forecast for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 calls for $38.15 in adjusted earnings per share, plus or minus $1. To hit $176, Micron would have to average around $46 a share in the three quarters after that, or about 21% over the guide. But growth is slowing. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 33% sequentially in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2026 (the period ending Sept. 3), and the guide implies a gain of around 14% in fiscal Q1. What's more, Micron's DRAM prices climbed by a high-teens percentage sequentially in fiscal Q4, down from a low-60s percentage gain in fiscal Q3.

To be fair, management expects sequential revenue growth in every quarter of fiscal 2027 and called fiscal Q1 the low for gross margin this fiscal year. But it's still a lot of growth to rely on from a product whose price can drop fast.

Micron's own history shows the valuation investors have paid when memory profits were booming. The stock closed at $62.62 on May 29, 2018, its peak for that cycle. That was about 5 times what the company ultimately earned on an adjusted basis in fiscal 2018 ($11.95 per share).

In its next boom, the stock closed at $97.36 on Jan. 14, 2022, or around 12 times what it later earned on an adjusted basis in fiscal 2022 ($8.35 per share).

The gap seems to boil down to how high profits had risen. Micron's adjusted gross margin was 59% in fiscal 2018, versus 46% in fiscal 2022.

And investors had good reason to doubt those profits. After all, adjusted earnings per share dropped 47% to $6.35 in fiscal 2019, and fiscal 2023 saw an adjusted loss of $4.45 per share.

Today's profits look much higher than either. Micron's adjusted gross margin reached 87% in fiscal Q4, up from 46% a year before. I'd lean closer to 2018's price-to-earnings ratio and use around 6 times fiscal 2027 earnings.

I'd go a bit over 2018's level because Micron arguably has more protection this time. It has signed 26 multiyear strategic customer agreements, with customers agreeing to $32 billion in financial commitments, primarily cash deposits.

Six times $176 comes to about $1,056, which I'd round down to $1,050. That's roughly 13% below the stock's June record close, so Micron wouldn't have to hit a new high for me to think it's too expensive.

My sell price tracks the estimate. Every $10 added to expected fiscal 2027 earnings per share would boost it by $60, so a strong fiscal Q1 report could raise it. If estimates fell to around $153 (the fiscal Q1 guide times four), my price would drop to about $920.

That price-to-earnings ratio could change too. If Micron's agreements covered much more of its revenue than they do today, I could justify paying more per dollar of earnings. And if DRAM prices start falling from quarter to quarter, I wouldn't wait for $1,050 at all.

For now, at around 4 times expected earnings, selling looks premature to me. Sure, there's no guarantee Micron hits $1,050 before profits start falling. I'd just keep close tabs on DRAM prices in the meantime.

Daniel Sparks and his clients do not have positions in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3066. OraSure (OSUR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Ebola demand lifted sales, but cash flow breakeven timing slipped.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

OraSure Technologies, Inc. (OSUR +2.62%) reported its results for the third quarter of 2026, noting a return to growth driven by expanded diagnostics and sample management portfolios. Management indicated that core business performance was supported by stabilization in international markets and demand for syndemic testing in the United States. The company is currently navigating the regulatory process for its molecular self-testing product while launching new diagnostic tools for Ebola and urine-based STI collection. Strategy for the upcoming year involves prioritizing operational efficiency and manufacturing consolidation to support a path toward positive operating cash flow.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the OraSure Technologies, Inc. 2026 Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this call may be recorded. I would now like to turn the call over to Mike Vallie, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Mike Vallie: Good afternoon, and welcome to OraSure Technologies Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Participating in the call for OTI are Carrie Eglinton Manner, our President and Chief Executive Officer; and Ken McGrath, our Chief Financial Officer. As a reminder, today's webcast is being recorded, and the recording can be found on our Investor Relations website. Before we begin, you should know that this call may contain certain forward-looking statements, including statements with respect to revenues, expenses, profitability, earnings or loss per share, cash flows and other financial performance, product development, performance, shipments and markets, business plans, regulatory filings and approvals, expectations and strategies. Actual results could be significantly different.

Factors that could affect results are discussed more fully in OraSure's SEC filings, its annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, its quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and its other SEC filings. Although forward-looking statements help to provide more complete information about future prospects, listeners should keep in mind that forward-looking statements are based solely on information available to management as of today. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statements to reflect events or circumstances after this call. In addition, the call will also discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures.

A reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures is included in our earnings press release issued today, which is available on the Investor Relations section of our website. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Carrie.

Carrie Eglinton Manner: Thanks, Mike, and thank you to everyone for joining us. Today, I'll discuss some highlights from Q3 and provide updates on our key priorities for the balance of 2026 and our outlook for 2027. Q3 was another solid quarter of execution and our return to growth. We delivered 14% year-over-year growth and 1% sequential growth, meaningfully expanded gross margins and reduced operating spend, results driven by continued execution of our strategy. Continuing now with more on each of our portfolios. In International Diagnostics, our Q3 performance reflected our approach to stabilize, diversify and localize our business.

We are building on our long-standing leadership in HIV testing while expanding our portfolio and strengthening partnerships that broaden our reach and enable us to address critical public health needs across Africa, Latin America and other international markets. Starting with Ebola. As discussed last quarter, in July, we received FDA emergency use authorization for our OraQuick Ebola 2.0 rapid antigen test. The test detects all 4 Ebola virus species known to cause human disease, including Bundibugyo, the species responsible for the current outbreak. Since the outbreak began, its scale and geographic reach have increased dramatically. As of November 3, WHO reports that there are now more than 10,600 confirmed cases and nearly 5,200 deaths.

Transmission has spread across multiple provinces in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and across international borders, including the first recorded cases in Kenya's history as well as the case in Nigeria. Against this backdrop, the need for rapid decentralized diagnostic capacity is clear. Rapid testing can play an important role alongside surveillance, contact tracing, isolation and other public health measures to identify cases quickly and help interrupt chains of transmission. Our test is particularly well suited for point-of-need deployment with its low infrastructure needs, speed and ease of use. Following our FDA EUA, we have quickly fulfilled initial commercial orders for Ebola 2.0. We believe, however, that the more meaningful catalysts for broader adoption are still ahead of us.

One important catalyst will be the results of the BRIDGE Access Platform study, which we previously discussed. Led by Africa CDC and WHO with Unitaid support, the BRIDGE Access Study is independently evaluating diagnostic products for the current Bundibugyo outbreak with the evidence intended to inform Africa CDC recommendations as well as national and regional decisions regarding registration and introduction of diagnostic tests. This is an important example of how the public health environment in Africa is evolving post-pandemic and following the international aid cuts of 2025. African countries are increasingly focused on building greater self-reliance and locally led health security infrastructure.

Africa CDC itself has made local manufacturing, reduced dependency and greater health sovereignty central elements of its health security agenda. That evolution means adoption increasingly occurs through African-led country-specific pathways for evaluation, registration, procurement and deployment. These include new processes that are taking time even during an urgent outbreak, but they also reinforce the importance of the investments we have been making to localize our presence and capabilities in the region. To best serve Africa, OraSure has launched local assembly in Uganda, where our partner is already expanding access to our HIV products and has the potential to add Ebola and other products in the future. Nigeria is our next planned market for launching our localized approach in Africa.

We believe we are well positioned as the Ebola response moves into its next phase. CDC currently assesses the most likely near-term scenario as a very large, sustained outbreak with high-intensity transmission in multiple areas, underscoring the immediate and continued need for a range of effective diagnostic tools. Our product can play an important role on the front lines and porous borders of this outbreak. Our manufacturing capability is ready, and we bring decades of experience and partnerships to readily serve the region's needs. Beyond this outbreak, we believe rapid point-of-need diagnostics can become an increasingly important component of outbreak preparedness and response and that OraSure is ready and able to play a meaningful role as these pathways mature.

Moving to sickle cell disease. We continue to support growing awareness and expansion of newborn screening across Africa, where Africa CDC estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 babies are born with sickle cell disease each year. This momentum is driving increased demand for Sickle SCAN and our successful integration of BioMedomics is enabling us to leverage our international commercial infrastructure to broaden access in markets with significant unmet need. We are also building partnerships with national and local health programs to expand point-of-need testing. Our recently announced partnership in Nairobi is one example, focused on scaling Sickle SCAN across community health centers and bringing testing closer to patients.

At the same time, our participation in the World Coalition on Sickle Cell Disease connects OTI with leaders across government, health care and patient advocacy to advance earlier diagnosis and strengthen testing pathways. We believe these relationships and joint efforts can help create the conditions for broader adoption of solutions like Sickle SCAN over time. In summary, the ongoing progress of HIV, early momentum of Sickle SCAN, the potential of Ebola plus the launch of our partners' near-shoring operations reflect the continued evolution of our international diagnostics strategy. We are successfully and increasingly pairing differentiated point-of-need diagnostics with localized capabilities and strong partnerships to expand access, diversify our business and unlock new growth priorities.

Over time, we believe this approach can continue to broaden our global reach, strengthen our competitive position and enhance the durability of our growth. Switching to U.S. Diagnostics. We delivered strong year-over-year growth driven by strength in HCV, syphilis and the continued underlying demand for HIV testing. Our syndemic testing strategy continues to be an important differentiator for us. With rapid testing solutions for HIV, HCV and syphilis, we give customers a broader set of tools to reach populations that face multiple interconnected infectious disease risks. We're very pleased with the progress of this strategy and the clinical and economic value it can deliver for our customers and the communities they serve.

Turning to a regulatory process update on our InteliQuick CT/NG test on the Sherlock platform, intended as a first-of-its-kind rapid molecular self-test. We continue to work towards our resubmission with the FDA following our announcement of withdrawal in August. We are currently working within the pre-sub process, the aim of which is to align on the best path to regulatory access. We have valuable experience and feedback from our prior submission and are leveraging that and this pre-sub process to evaluate a range of pathways that can bring this important innovation to market. We remain confident in the product's performance, the impact it can have on patients and our ability to navigate the regulatory landscape.

We will provide updates as we have more to share. Now moving to our Sample Management Solutions portfolio. Growth from key commercial customers, along with the timing of orders, contributed to a strong Q3 with growth of more than 20%, both year-over-year and sequentially. As announced last quarter, we received FDA clearance for our Colli-Pee Dx urine collection kit in June. We believe this technology can help expand access to STI testing through a more convenient and private approach to sample collection. We commercially launched the product in the third quarter and have been very encouraged by initial sales.

At the same time, we are excited by the pipeline of potential customers who see real opportunities for the technology, both the chemistry and the device, with many evaluating the workflow required to incorporate self-collected urine into their testing programs. This customer engagement reinforces our confidence in the opportunity for Colli-Pee Dx to support expanded access to STI testing over time. In Q3, we delivered strong growth in our SMS portfolio. Looking forward, our robust portfolio, the increased anticipated contributions from Colli-Pee and its NucleoPrecision chemistry, along with our partnerships with IVD platform manufacturers, reinforce our confidence in the long-term outlook for Sample Management Solutions and its ability to contribute to our return to growth strategy.

Overall, as we've outlined, OTI delivered a solid third quarter. We further demonstrated our return to growth, drove meaningful gross margin expansion and continued to take cost out of the business. These results reflect the progress we are making in executing our strategy and positioning the business for sustainable growth and long-term value creation. With that, I'll turn the call over to Ken to discuss our financial results and guidance.

Kenneth McGrath: Thanks, Carrie. Total revenue in the third quarter was $30.9 million, growing 14% year-over-year and approximately 1% on a sequential basis. Diagnostic products generated $16.8 million of revenue in Q3, representing 16% year-over-year growth. The increase was driven by higher international HIV revenue, reflecting stabilization in our African markets and customer order timing, improved HCV performance supported by U.S. funding dynamics and continued growth from Sickle SCAN. Sample Management Solutions revenue in Q3 was $12.5 million, a 21% year-over-year increase, driven by key commercial customer growth and timing of specific commercial orders. Our Q3 GAAP gross margin increased 173 basis points to 45.2% from 43.5% in the third quarter of last year.

And non-GAAP gross margin in Q3 increased to 45.9% from 44.2%. The gross margin expansion was driven by operational efficiencies, resulting in improved overhead absorption, partially offset by geographic mix. While margins may move quarter-to-quarter based on product mix and order timing, we believe the absorption gains we have built this year will continue to further improve as we scale the business. Turning to operating expenses. As expected, we saw a material sequential improvement in our operating spend. In the third quarter, R&D expense was $7.6 million, down $1.8 million sequentially as a result of the tapering of development-related spend.

At the same time, we continue to invest in innovation, including advancing the early development of HPV testing as a potential future application for Colli-Pee in collaboration with leading global molecular diagnostic partners. Sales and marketing remained relatively flat at $6.6 million as we leverage our existing capabilities to invest in new growth within our portfolio. And finally, as expected, G&A expense declined to a more normalized level in the third quarter. Total G&A was $12 million, a significant $2.4 million reduction coming as a result of lower nonrecurring items, including legal and professional service costs. Noncash stock compensation expense in the third quarter was $2.3 million, and depreciation and amortization expense was $2.2 million.

And our GAAP operating income in Q3 was a loss of $13 million, and our non-GAAP operating loss was $10.2 million. Moving to our balance sheet. We ended the quarter with 0 debt and total cash and cash equivalents of $148.2 million. Operating cash flow in the third quarter was negative $10.9 million. Consistent with our balanced capital deployment strategy, we continue to evaluate organic and inorganic opportunities that can accelerate our profitable growth in high-value markets and leverage our existing capabilities. On the partnership front, Sapphiros KKR announced last week that it combined with Hildred-backed binx health to form Onvaro.

Through our existing investment in Sapphiros, OraSure remains a minority investor in the combined company, and our strategic agreements with Sapphiros remain in place. Next, moving to guidance. In the fourth quarter, we expect revenue between $30 million and $32 million, which would represent year-over-year growth of approximately 12% to 20% in the quarter. This guidance represents full year revenue between $119.5 million and $121.5 million and implies a full year growth rate between 3.8% and 5.6%, with 4.7% at the midpoint and as we expect gross margin in Q4 to be similar to or slightly below Q3.

As I mentioned earlier, while quarterly margins may fluctuate due to revenue mix, improved manufacturing efficiencies and continued focus on our underlying margin profile are driving fundamental improvement and providing a stronger base to build from going forward. Looking ahead to 2027. Regarding cash flow from operations. At the beginning of the year, we laid out a path to achieving cash flow from operations breakeven, entering 2027. That plan contemplated a combination of continued improvement in the underlying business and contributions from several growth opportunities. As the year progressed, the timing and mix of those growth opportunities have changed. Our original plan included a meaningful contribution from CT/NG molecular self-testing.

Following our decision to withdraw that submission, we had identified other opportunities, including significant potential demand for Ebola rapid testing that we believe could offset much of the contribution within the original time frame. As Carrie discussed, we continue to see attractive opportunities in Ebola and across the broader portfolio. But as the timing of these opportunities has evolved, we have decided to take a more conservative approach to our estimates, and we now expect to reach cash flow from operations breakeven in the second half of 2027. Continuing our conversation on 2027.

In alignment with the execution of our strategy, we expect full year revenue growth to accelerate in 2027 compared with 2026, and we'll provide additional insights into our 2027 outlook on our fourth quarter earnings call. With that, I'll turn the call back to Carrie to conclude.

Carrie Eglinton Manner: Thanks, Ken. Looking to the balance of 2026 and into 2027, we are focused on continued execution of our strategy and our return to profitable growth. During the third quarter, we demonstrated the results of our strategy, supported by our simplified portfolio, operating discipline, strengthened production and manufacturing capabilities and advanced innovation pipeline. Together, these drivers translate to revenue and operating margin expansion, positioning OraSure to deliver sustainable long-term value for our customers, partners and shareholders. Thank you for your continued support and confidence in OTI. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to the operator for Q&A. Michelle?

Carrie Eglinton Manner: Yes. Mac, we'll start with just following on from our prepared remarks. We are in the pre-sub process on CT/NG. We think there's really a range of potential paths forward. Carrie Eglinton Manner: And just to put maybe a little bit finer point on Q3 and Q4. John Wilkin: That makes sense. Fair enough. And then lastly, I just want to ask you, if you're able to delve any more into just what the contracting process is looking like for Ebola. And I know you mentioned a couple of countries in the pipeline that you're going to be launching into.
